title: Has Bo Nix quieted early-season criticisms ahead of Las Vegas Raiders-Denver Broncos Week 11 matchup?
summary: Week 11 reignites a longstanding AFC West rivalry between the Las Vegas Raiders and Denver Broncos. To preview the game, Silver and Black Pride reached out to our frenemies at Mile High Report, and Ian St. Clair was kind enough to answer a few questions about the Broncos for Raider Nation. Q: Bo Nix faced […]
full_text: (Photo by Ian Maule/Getty Images) | Getty Images Week 11 reignites a longstanding AFC West rivalry between the Las Vegas Raiders and Denver Broncos . To preview the game, Silver and Black Pride reached out to our frenemies at Mile High Report, and Ian St. Clair was kind enough to answer a few questions about the Broncos for Raider Nation. Q: Bo Nix faced a lot of criticism at the beginning of the season for not pushing the ball down the field. Has that changed over the last handful of games? Is ending last season with a broken ankle impacting how he’s been playing in 2026? A: No matter what happens on the field, Nix is one of those players who will always face criticism. It’s also important to add some context for why things may unfold on the field over the course of a game. Early in the season, Nix and the Broncos offense played some of the best defenses in the NFL. On top of that, Denver’s running game was horrendous, and that’s even putting it mildly. Opposing defenses knew they could stop the Broncos rushing attack with minimal effort and play two-high safeties. In situations like that, it’s going to be hard for a quarterback or offense to push the ball down the field. However, Nix and Denver did open it up a bit more against the Carolina Panthers. Early in the game, Nix took some deep shots that set up the offense for points. We will likely see a continuation of that this Sunday. As for Nix’s injury, there’s no doubt it impacted him earlier in the season. I’d say more so mentally than physically. All the physical rehab in the world doesn’t rehab the mind until you actually do it and prove to yourself that you can do it. The last few games have been more like the Nix we saw before the injury, and belief and confidence are reemerging. Q: On a related note, Jaylen Waddle was the Broncos’ biggest offseason addition but has just 30 catches for 337 yards and two touchdowns through nine games. What were the expectations for Waddle heading into the season, and what’s been holding him back from meeting them? A: The expectations were high that Waddle would bring an element to Denver’s offense that would open it up. Nix and the Broncos would be able to take deep shots and use his speed in the middle of the field. It’s been surprising how inconsistent that has been thus far. We’ve seen flashes, but not nearly enough. Obviously, what I mentioned earlier with the focus opposing defenses can put on the passing game plays into that, but it’s also not utilizing him properly. Plus, the fact that Nix has been inconsistent and struggled hasn’t helped. Coming out of the bye, I think we’ll start to see Waddle play a bigger role in the Broncos offense. Q: Who would you say is more important to Denver’s defense and why: Nik Bonitto or Pat Surtain II? A: My answer might change in five minutes, but I’ll go with Bonitto. Mind you, I think that Surtain is the best cornerback in football. He’s one of those cornerbacks who shuts down half the field. However, having a game-changing edge rusher in Bonitto sets the rest of the defense up for success, including Surtain. What Bonitto brings and how effective he is reminds me of Von Miller, who was the Super Bowl 50 MVP. At any moment, Bonitto can make a play that changes a game. Or, in the case against the Panthers, win it. He’s become one of the best edge players in the league, and he just brings so much to the Broncos’ defense. Q: Seahawks head coach/defensive play caller Mike Macdonald gave Fernando Mendoza trouble last week by throwing the book at the rookie with several exotic pressure looks. Should Mendoza expect the same from Vance Joseph this week? What can you tell us about Joseph’s scheme that could give a quarterback making his second career start fits? A: The scheme is only as good as the players who execute it, and that’s where I think Mendoza will face similar challenges this Sunday. Denver is one of the best defenses in the NFL, if not the best, at pressuring the quarterback. Even if Joseph doesn’t call a blitz, the Broncos front will still make life miserable for Mendoza with Bonitto, Jonathan Cooper, Zack Allen, and Co. But then there are the times Joseph will send a cornerback or safety on a blitz out of package that Mendoza isn’t expecting. But the biggest reason Mendoza will face pressure is the Raiders’ currently ineffective running game. Being one-dimensional on offense is never a friend to a rookie quarterback making his second start against a great defense. Q: Can you give us one player on each side of the ball who Raider Nation might not know much about but could make an impact in this game? A couple of the Broncos’ up-and-comers, if you will . A: On offense, let’s go with rookie running back Jonah Coleman. Though I’m pretty sure Las Vegas fans know of Coleman. But he is what makes Denver’s running game click. Coleman’s has good vision, good speed, and runs with power. He’s been fun to watch, and I would expect him to get more carries on Sunday. On defense, there really isn’t anybody who Raiders Nation hasn’t heard of. So I’ll go with cornerback Ja’Quan McMillian. The fourth-year undrafted defensive back has a knack for making a key play when Denver needs it, whether an interception or a sack.

title: Division games a true barometer of Raiders progress, or lack of it
summary: Divisional games just hit different in the NFL. Featuring the twice-a-year meetings which lead to some heated rematches, the weight division games carry are much heavier than the standard affair of matchups league schedule makers put forth amongst the 32 teams. When the AFC and NFC teams in the East, North, South, and West tango, […]
full_text: (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images Divisional games just hit different in the NFL. Featuring the twice-a-year meetings which lead to some heated rematches, the weight division games carry are much heavier than the standard affair of matchups league schedule makers put forth amongst the 32 teams. When the AFC and NFC teams in the East, North, South, and West tango, the playoff stakes are higher (I’ll explain this more below) alongside familiarity creating either nail-biter meetings lopsided beatdowns. It’ll be intriguing to see which way the Las Vegas Raiders road trip to the Denver Broncos this Sunday plays out. Will it be an AFC West slugfest that’s close? Or will the bucking Broncos trample the visiting Raiders? With four of the final seven games on Las Vegas’ slate being AFC West tilts — at Denver this Sunday; hosting the Los Angeles Chargers (Week 14, Dec. 13); hosting the Broncos (Week 15, Dec. 20); and at the Kansas City Chiefs (Week 18, Jan. 10) — we’re going to see how much progress Klint Kubiak’s Raiders have made — or the lack of it. Kubiak, the heralded offensive mind who the Silver & Black tabbed as its 27th head coach in franchise history, has a storied history with Denver as he grew up around the team thanks to his father Gary, who spent decades as a Broncos player, offensive coordinator, head coach, and senior personnel advisory. “Yeah, many memories. Looking forward to going back to the stadium and being a part of this game. Extremely excited for our team,” the stoic younger Klint Kubiak said when asked about a memory that stands out as he heads back to Denver, this time, as a rookie head coach. “I think when I was blessed enough to get hired here to coach the Raiders, I thought about games in Denver and games in Kansas City and being a part of this division, so it’s something that I’ve definitely thought about before. And now that we’re in it, we’re in the season. It’s just next practice.” Kubiak is set to lead his 4-6 Raiders against Sean Peyton’s 7-2 Broncos highlighting the different spectrums of success the two division foes are currently at. A win keeps Denver in-line with the 7-2 Chiefs and an all-important AFC West title and high seed in the postseason race. A victory by Las Vegas puts a nice shiner on Denver’s division title hunt. "They always show up and play the Broncos hard." 🗣️ Courtland Sutton on facing Klint Kubiak and the @Raiders #broncoscountry pic.twitter.com/PhCfC2g1p5 — Guerilla Sports (@guerillasports) November 19, 2026 As Broncos wide receiver Courtland Sutton aptly mentioned above, the division games often lead to close, hard-fought one-score contests because teams know each other so well that tendencies are identified and counters properly installed. Even when one team is the cellar desperately trying to climb out, it can give a team atop the mountain with lofty goals in their eyes a difficult time gameday. This is a direct result of that deep familiarity and competitive drive amongst players and coaches. As they say, familiarity breeds contempt and there’s no love lost between the Raiders and Broncos — heck, the entire AFC West. Las Vegas intends to be in the spot Denver is now — fighting for the division crown, a ticket to the postseason dance, and a legitimate chase for another Lombardi Trophy — and the future is now as the team traded trusty veteran Kirk Cousins and are now on the Fernando Mendoza era at quarterback. The rookie and No. 1 overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft is well aware of what Week 11 presents for the Silver & Black. “It’s a great challenge. It’s a rivalry game. If you can’t get excited for a rivalry game, then there might be something wrong with you,” Mendoza said. “So, I’m incredibly excited to take on the challenge. They’re a great opponent. They have a great team. They have a great coach and a great quarterback. So, I’m looking forward to taking it on with my teammates.” Through the 10 games the Raiders have played this season, the team is 1-1 in AFC West play (beat the Chargers 26-14 in Week 2; lost to the Chiefs 30-27 in Week 4) and are 3-3 against AFC foes. The Broncos, on the other hand, are coming off their bye week and are 2-1 in division games played (lost the Chiefs 31-10 in Week 1; beat the Chargers 23-17 in Week 5, topped the Chiefs 28-24 in Week 8) and are 3-1 in AFC play through their nine games on the year. I hate the fact I don’t hate the @Raiders with the same hate I once hated the @Raiders . pic.twitter.com/IpBCVTDkLJ — Vic Lombardi (@VicLombardi) November 16, 2026 Kubiak needs to get complementary football from his Raiders where his offense combines with Rob Leonard’s defense, and Joe DeCamillis’ special teams unit to lift each unit up against a Broncos team eyeing back-to-back AFC West titles, something the Chiefs won nine-straight seasons from 2016-2024. “Yeah, absolutely. Obviously, I’ve learned how big of an operation this is, and how it takes a team to go win a football game,” Kubiak said on what he’s learned about himself 10 games into his head coaching career. “It’s every week I’m learning new things. But the great thing about this whole experience is surrounding yourself with excellent people, and from our personnel staff to our coaching staff to our players, I could not have come into a better situation with the type of people.” Sunday marks a first for Mendoza, too. “Yeah, it’s going to be very loud. They have a great fan base, and that’s something we’ve been practicing at practice, whether it’s the crowd noise, to make sure we get adjusted to that. It’s going to be a great environment,” the rookie said. “But it is new. I’ve never started on the road before, so I’m looking forward to the challenge.” Quotes of Note “Protection is an all 11 thing. It’s everybody. The run game is an all 11 thing. That’s the greatest thing about football; is every play all 11 people are involved. It’s not just one person making a play. It’s all 11 coming together for success. So, everybody has a role in a touchdown play. Everybody has a role in a sack. Everybody has a role in an explosive run. Everybody has a role in a tackle for loss. So, specifically, you look at each individual play and you coach every single position on how can we get better in that circumstance to make that play successful.” —Las Vegas Raiders offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko on the shared responsibility of accounting for cornerback blitzes “Yeah, at times. We’re not playing well enough. We’re not playing up to the standard we need to be. So, effort covers up a lot. So, there’s definitely room for improvement there. And to say it’s division from the start, no, we’re not playing at a high enough or good enough level right now. So, there’s definitely room for improvement.” —Las Vegas Raiders defensive coordinator Rob Leonard on how the fast and aggressive play style he wants from his defenders has translated into game days

title: Raiders Mailbag: How will Fernando Mendoza look in 2nd career start against Denver Broncos’ defense?
summary: Fernando Mendoza had an up-and-down performance in his first career start against the Seattle Seahawks last week, and his second start comes against the Denver Broncos’ defense, which led the NFL in sacks during the 2024 and 2025 campaigns. So, there’s a lot of talk about the Las Vegas Raiders’ Week 11 matchup and the […]
full_text: (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images Fernando Mendoza had an up-and-down performance in his first career start against the Seattle Seahawks last week, and his second start comes against the Denver Broncos’ defense , which led the NFL in sacks during the 2024 and 2025 campaigns. So, there’s a lot of talk about the Las Vegas Raiders’ Week 11 matchup and the rookie quarterback in this week’s mailbag. Let’s get to it! A: The Broncos’ defense definitely isn’t as dominant as we’ve seen over the last two years, ranking 27th in yards per game allowed ( 355.0 ) and 13th in EPA per play (-0.05) allowed, per Sumer Sports . Granted, the latter is just outside the top third of the league, but that’s below the standard Denver has set recently. So, I think Mendoza can have more success and should have an easier time moving the ball this Sunday compared to last week. The biggest area he needs to improve on is handling pressure. Broncos defensive coordinator Vance Joseph is different from Seahawks head coach/defensive play caller Mike Macdonald, in that Macdonald leans more on creating confusion through varying pre-snap looks and simulated pressures (showing blitz but rushing four). Joseph will line up and play more, letting Denver’s excellent pass-rushers pin their ears back and do their jobs. But he isn’t afraid to bring the heat either, ranking 11th with a 33.7 percent blitz rate, according to Sumer . Especially after watching last week, I’d expect Joseph to dive deep into the playbook and continue to throw the kitchen sink at the rookie quarterback making his second career start. So, it’s going to be important for Mendoza to stay poised under pressure and be faster at finding his answers/check downs. I have confidence that he’ll be able to make an adjustment; poise and toughness in the pocket were two of his biggest strengths last year at Indiana. However, of course, it’s a whole different ball game at this level, and he needs to prove it on the field. The good news is that it should be all downhill from here as far as facing strong defenses with very good pass-rushers for the rest of the season. Well, until the Raiders play the Broncos again in a few weeks, LOL! A: I’m definitely on board with you that Klint Kubiak has to reverse script and use the passing game to set up the rushing attack. Also, I think you’re onto something about that being the strategy last week, where the first two plays of the game were play-action bootlegs. The next four plays were runs (one three-yarder and three four-yarders) to keep the offense on schedule, and then another play-action bootleg. As you mentioned, Brock Bowers going down changed the strategy, or at least the effectiveness of it. Also, Macdonald started giving Mendoza the confusing pressure looks toward the end of the second quarter, making the problem even worse. It sounds like Bowers will at least be out there on Sunday ( he’s currently listed as questionable ) to make the Broncos account for him, so I’d expect Kubiak to use a similar strategy. Hopefully, the ‘football robot from heaven’ is healthy enough to be effective and can stay on the field to give us a full game to see how using the pass to set up the run works with Mendoza behind center. Q: When you think about QB skill sets and what can or can’t be developed effectively, where does pocket presence fall? Not going to lie, Mendoza’s pocket presence troubles me a bit going back to Indiana. A: Mendoza’s feel for pressure was/is definitely one of my biggest concerns about his transition to the NFL. Where it can get complicated is that it’s tied to his fearlessness under pressure. He’s tough as hell and has no problem standing tall and making throws while taking a hit in the pocket. But the downside is that he will stay in the pocket too long and take sacks, some of those being big hits from free rushers. I flinched on both of Devon Witherspoon’s sacks last week. LOL! So, it’s one of those things where Fernando is going to have to find the balance between one of his biggest strengths and one of his biggest weaknesses. You don’t want him to become timid and turn into a ‘Checkdown Charlie’. However, six sacks a game will lead to a short career. Ultimately, the only way to find the balance is to get live reps in games since the defense isn’t hitting the quarterback in practice. Jordan Love had a similar problem when he first became the Packers’ starter, taking 29 sacks with a 15.2 percent pressure-to-sack ratio, per Pro Football Focus . In year two, Love’s figures went down to 14 and 8.9 percent, and then 21 and 10.9 percent last season. Granted, this season he’s back up to 25 and 15.8 percent, but 12 sacks came in two games against the Vikings. That’s just par for the course against Brian Flores, especially with how that defense has been playing this year. I’d be willing to bet Love’s pressure-to-sack percentage comes down by the end of the year. In other words, it’s something that can be improved. Mendoza just has to get more reps and make an adjustment to have a better feel for pressure. Personally, I think it’s easier to coach a quarterback to get the ball out faster than it is to force a scared quarterback to be braver in the pocket. One is a timing issue, and the other requires a rewiring of the brain, so to speak. Quick break to let you guys know about a new release from Homage. Follow this link to get your Raiders Blackout Starter Jacket ! HOMAGE x Starter Raiders Blackout Breakaway Pullover Jacket Q: It might be way too early for this question: Xavier Gilliam, Zereoue Williams, Jackson Harris, and Will Echoles are there for a first-round pick. What’s your choice? The team needs WR and IDL talent badly, but may also need to look at a future replacement for Kolton Miller soon. A: You’re scratching the surface on an offseason topic that will likely be heavily talked about: Is it time to move on from Miller? I wouldn’t say he’s been bad by any means, but the 31-year-old has certainly regressed this season to the point where finding a long-term blind-side protector will be on the table. So, someone like Williams or Jordan Seaton (if the Raiders are picking high enough) could be an option in the first round. However, right now, I’m willing to give Miller the rest of the campaign before closing the book on him and creating a new need in Las Vegas’ trenches. On that note, the Raiders need to get better on both sides of the trenches before worrying about adding a wide receiver, in my opinion. The only caveat to that would be if they’re in range for Jeremiah Smith (highly unlikely) or Charlie Becker (fairly unlikely). Outside of those two, there isn’t a receiver in this class who stands out enough to push me away from a lineman. I think there should be good/better value at wide receiver in the second round this year. So, it comes down to Gilliam or Echoles. To be honest, I’d be pretty happy with either, but I lean toward Echoles. Gilliam has undoubtedly been the better player this year and has the potential to be an impact player against the run and as an interior pass-rusher. However, he is a one-year wonder, so Echoles has the bigger body of work, and I trust him against the run more. The Ole Miss product definitely has to be more consistent as a pass-rusher, but the flashes are there to show some potential to grow in that department. But, again, I’d be pretty happy if the Raiders managed to land either of those defensive tackles. Q: What is the difference between this year’s Ashton Jeanty and last year’s Ashton Jeanty? A: To me, Jeanty doesn’t have the same lateral movement skills and shiftiness that he showed as a rookie. Granted, those were never his biggest strengths, but I feel like his jump cuts and ability to make defenders miss have regressed this season. The straight-line speed and burst are still there, as seen in last week’s 38-yard catch. However, Pro Football Focus had him with 61 missed tackles forced in 17 games last year (about 3.6 a…

title: Las Vegas Raiders-Denver Broncos FEED Topic: Kolton Miller, DJ Glaze vs. Nik Bonitto, Jonathon Cooper
summary: The Seattle Seahawks managed to get six sacks on Fernando Mendoza in his starting debut last week, and pressure on the quarterback will be another major key to the game for the Las Vegas Raiders’ offense in Week 11. The Denver Broncos present the same problem but in a different way than Seattle, one that […]
full_text: (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Seattle Seahawks managed to get six sacks on Fernando Mendoza in his starting debut last week , and pressure on the quarterback will be another major key to the game for the Las Vegas Raiders’ offense in Week 11. The Denver Broncos present the same problem but in a different way than Seattle, one that will place a greater emphasis on the Raiders’ offensive line, especially tackles Kolton Miller and DJ Glaze . Led by head coach Mike Macdonald, the Seahawks defense uses a creative scheme to help manufacture pressure and create confusion for opposing quarterbacks. To a certain extent, they’re able to work around or neutralize the offensive line by attacking running backs in pass protection or forcing quarterbacks to account for free rushers by throwing hot. Last week was a perfect example, as top cornerback Devon Witherspoon led the team with two of the six sacks. Meanwhile, Broncos defensive coordinator Vance Joseph isn’t afraid to blitz, but that’s to help create one-on-one opportunities for their defensive linemen, especially edge rushers Nik Bonitto and Jonathon Cooper. Bonitto is coming off back-to-back Pro Bowl seasons, where he registered 27.5 sacks and 133 pressures, per Pro Football Focus , in 2024 and 2025 combined. This season, he’s recorded 4.5 sacks in nine games and ranks tied for 19th among edges with 30 pressures . Meanwhile, Cooper notched 18.5 sacks and 112 pressures in the two previous seasons to give the Broncos a quality No. 2 pass-rusher on the edge. In 2026, he’s only participated in three games due to off-field issues in the offseason and has just 10 pressures and 0.5 sacks on 77 pass-rush snaps. So, Cooper’s numbers are down as a consequence of his actions, but his track record on the field speaks for itself. On the other side of the trenches, Miller has an impressive resume in pass protection but has been regressing this year. With 32 pressures on 379 opportunities, per PFF , his 8.4 percent pressure rate is the highest it’s been since the 2018 first-round pick’s rookie year (11.0 percent). But Glaze is trending in the opposite direction, going from 8.3 percent and 8.0 percent pressure rates in his first two seasons, respectively, to 4.0 percent ( 15 pressures on 379 opportunities ) this year. With the Raiders shifting from Kirk Cousins to Mendoza last week and seeing their playoff hopes rapidly decline over the last roughly two months, we’ve reached the point in the season where it’s time to start looking at building for the future. Part of that is making sure the rookie quarterback can stay upright enough to make some plays and build confidence heading into next year. The other part is evaluating the team’s needs before the offseason gets going. It would be remiss to talk about the Broncos’ pass rush and not mention Zach Allen, who currently leads all defensive tackles with 38 pressures and has 4.5 sacks . However, it feels like a foregone conclusion that Las Vegas will have to address its guard situation this spring. Meanwhile, offensive tackle is still up in the air, and this weekend will be a good litmus test for Miller and Glaze. Is the veteran left tackle past his prime, where it’s time to find a new blind side protector? Is the third-year pro’s growth legitimate? How they fare against one of the NFL’s best edge-rush duos over the last few years, Bonitto and Cooper, on Sunday will go a long way toward answering those questions. So, for this week’s game day discussion on The FEED , we’ll be keeping tabs on how well Miller and Glaze can protect the edges to keep Mendoza clean in Denver. The game kicks off at 1:25 p.m. PST and will air on CBS (check your local listings). I look forward to talkin’ some ball with y’all!

title: Raiders Week 11: Fernando Mendoza’s arm, legs key against stingy Broncos
summary: With just 186 total points allowed in nine games, the Denver Broncos boast the ninth-best defensive unit in that regard, which will make it tough sledding for the Las Vegas Raiders this Sunday. The Silver & Black Express rolls into Mile High with a new conductor in prized rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza a road divisional […]
full_text: (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images With just 186 total points allowed in nine games, the Denver Broncos boast the ninth-best defensive unit in that regard, which will make it tough sledding for the Las Vegas Raiders this Sunday. The Silver & Black Express rolls into Mile High with a new conductor in prized rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza a road divisional matchup against the first-place Broncos (tied with the Kansas City Chiefs at 7-2 overall). The No. 1 overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft, Mendoza made his first career start against the stifling Seattle Seahawks defense and Las Vegas fell 21-13 in Week 10. Another formidable defense awaits Mendoza in Week 11 as Vance Joseph’s Denver squad comes off a bye week after a wire-to-wire Week 9 26-21 win at the Carolina Panthers two Sunday’s ago. To hear the 23-year-old budding franchise quarterback tell it, however, he wouldn’t have it any other way as he preps for his second-career NFL start this Sunday in Denver. “I believe getting thrown in the fire is the best way to learn, and the Seahawks and the Broncos both have considerably elite defenses,” Mendoza said when asked what it’s like getting thrown into the fire against two quality NFL defenses. “I really believe every NFL defense is elite because when you’re playing at this level, the margin for error is so small, and all the defensive coordinators are geniuses. “So, I’m honored and blessed to go against a great defensive coordinator in Coach Robbie (Raiders defensive coordinator Rob Leonard) every single day, especially in OTAs and fall camp and training camp. So, I believe that’s helped prepare me, an now I’m excited to embark on this journey with my teammates.” #Broncos ’ Bo Nix on peaking at the right time and how different the QB experience is when making 44th start compared to second like #Raiders ’ Fernando Mendoza pic.twitter.com/kvgaDzKQ2y — Troy Renck (@TroyRenck) November 18, 2026 How Mendoza settles during his second start against an aggressive Broncos defense bears watching. The Seahawks produced a blueprint of how to and how not to defend the Indiana product last week. When protected with a clean (and sometimes noisy) pocket, Mendoza was a smooth operator going through progressions and using his accurate and strong arm to deliver the football to Raiders pass catchers. In the first half, Mendoza went 11-of-13 for 90 yards including his first-career touchdown run. When Seattle saw enough of that, head coach and defensive play caller Mike Macdonald went to his bag of tricks of blitz, simulated pressure, and exotic alignments to take advantage of the neophyte signal caller and Mendoza went 6-of-16 for 53 yards in the second half while absorbing six sacks and 12 hits. Expect Joseph to stick to a similar script and bring the pain on the 6-foot-5 and 225-pound Raiders quarterback. Especially considering the Broncos have 84 quarterback hits on the season alongside 26 sacks. Zach Allen is an ultra-productive defensive lineman who plays both inside as a tackle and outside as an edge rusher and paces Denver with 4.5 sacks and 23 quarterback hits. Edge rusher Nik Bonitto is right there with him with 4.5 sacks and 11 QB hits while defensive tackle Malcolm Roach is disruptive with four sacks and 13 quarterback hits. Heat-seeking inside linebacker Alex Singleton is a quality clean-up man and is tied for the league lead in tackles at 107 (Raiders inside linebacker Nakobe Dean is who he is tied with) and also has two sacks and six quarterback hits on his stat sheet. All of this is presented to note Mendoza’s accurate arm and fresh legs are integral to Las Vegas’ aspirations to walk out of Denver with an AFC West win. That dual-threat ability is essential to counter the Joseph’s defense that is every bit as creative and chaotic as Macdonald’s group. All it takes is a few successful scrambles to make a defense bite — Seattle did this — and with Mendoza lauded for his cerebral ways and ability to not make the same mistake again, watching the film from last Sunday’s loss will showcase just that. The second-quarter 22-yard dart Mendoza zipped to wide receiver Cody White is an example of this. Mendoza felt pressure, began to scramble but kept his eyes downfield, and his ability to thrown on the arm and velocity on the fast ball were on full display. Fernando Mendoza ➡️ Cody White for the first down! SEAvsLV on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/KmbkHKSAKr — NFL (@NFL) November 15, 2026 “We have a great strength and conditioning staff here, and performance staff as a whole, whether it’s the training staff, nutrition, strength. There’s so many different aspects of it, so I’m blessed to be a part of it,” Mendoza began when as he answered a question about his mobility being an underrated aspect of his game, “I believe I’ve gotten faster since being here, and I’m grateful for that because in the NFL, those players are fast.” Those fleet feet will come in handy to escape the exotic blitzes Joseph is expected to deploy. Especially with Las Vegas ground game grinding to a halt consistently over the course of the 2026 season, much to the chagrin of Raiders rookie head coach and offensive play caller Klint Kubiak. Mendoza’s ability to run helps provide an alternative run game and scrambling for hidden yards and first downs can frustrate the opposing defense. Kubiak should again go play-action heavy with designed rollouts and bootlegs to vary the launch point of the ball and give his talented rookie cleaner passing lane and run-pass options. Mendoza has the arm talent to push the ball downfield and by getting the ball into the hands of his pass catchers quickly or downfield, Las Vegas can take advantage of Denver’s penchant to whiff on tackles as the team has a high 16.2 percent missed tackle rate. Of course, it’d help to have a healthy Brock Bowers available as the tight end is the Raiders’ de facto WR1. Mendoza is keen on balancing staying in the pocket and winning with this arm while also knowing when to run and gain positive yards against Denver. “There were a lot of moments in the game that we reviewed after in the film, whether it’s Coach Kubiak, Coach (Andrew) Janocko or Coach (Mike) Sullivan, they made comments on whatever the situation was, whether it was some inefficiency or a play that in the future we want to change. So, I’m taking those day by day and trying to improve on them,” Mendoza said regarding staying in the pocket longer to deliver a throw instead of taking off as quickly as he did in his first start. Listen to what the support from Raider Nation means to Fernando Mendoza (Via CBS, @mickakers ) pic.twitter.com/esG3mYtH5F — FOX Sports: NFL (@NFLonFOX) November 16, 2026 While the Broncos boast the ninth-best red zone defense — teams have visited the space between the 20-yard line and end zone 29 times for only 15 touchdowns for a 51.7 percent conversion rate — they are susceptible to getting yards piled upon them allowing 3,195 yards for 27th most amongst the 32 teams. That right there is a textbook example of a bend-but-not-break defense. Head-to-Head Sunday’s Mile High tilt marks the 134th time the Raiders and Broncos go toe-to-toe. The Silver & Black lead the all-time series 73-58-2 (72-5702 in regular season play, 1-1 in the playoffs) but are riding a four-game losing skid against the Horsemen. The last time Las Vegas beat Denver was in January of 2024, a 27-14 victory inside Allegiant Stadium. Since that tilt, the Broncos have won the next four meetings 34-18, 29-19, 10-7, and 24-17. The pair of longtime AFC West foes will meet again in Week 15 in Las Vegas. Quotes of Note “We were in a zone, it was an extended play, and expecting a quick throw and it became something — when extended plays happen, we always talk about the second play, and plaster, and those types of things. Anytime something doesn’t go well I wish I would have called something different.” —Las Vegas Raiders defensive coordinator Rob Leonard…

title: Dolphins fan confidence stumbles after Colts loss with Bills looming in Week 11
summary: The Miami Dolphins fell 24-22 to the Indianapolis Colts in Week 10, dropping them to 1-8 for the year. They now face an uphill battle as they start their home-and-home series with the Buffalo Bills, beginning in Week 11 with a visit to western New York. Whereas Miami is in a battle for the top […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - NOVEMBER 15: Caleb Douglas #7 and Jalen Tolbert #1 of the Miami Dolphins celebrate a touchdown during the first half against the Indianapolis Colts at Lucas Oil Stadium on November 15, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Michael Hickey/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Miami Dolphins fell 24-22 to the Indianapolis Colts in Week 10, dropping them to 1-8 for the year. They now face an uphill battle as they start their home-and-home series with the Buffalo Bills, beginning in Week 11 with a visit to western New York. Whereas Miami is in a battle for the top spot in the 2027 NFL Draft, the Bills are positioning themselves to be the best team in the AFC playoff picture. This week’s game is one where just about everything favors Buffalo. Can Miami be the David to the Bills’ Goliath? The latest FanDuel Sportsbook odds do not think so, with Buffalo favored by 16.5 points as of Saturday afternoon. Dolphins fan confidence Miami’s 2026 season is clearly a rebuild, with the team stripping the roster to the bare bones in the offseason, then restocking it with rookies, first- and second-year players, and journeyman veterans on one-year prove-it contracts. They are reframing the team and the philosophy surrounding it, shaking the finesse persona that dominated the Mike McDaniel era and taking on a new one under head coach Jeff Hafley. The fans have, for the most part this season, recognized that the wins and losses in 2026 do not matter, as long as the team seems to be growing and developing. This season will put Miami in a position to compete in 2027 and beyond. One year of pain before, hopefully, starting to see the fruits of the team’s labor. Last week, heading into the game against the Colts, our weekly SB Nation Reacts fan confidence poll showed 91 percent of the fans believed Miami was headed in the right direction. After the Colts loss, and with the Bills looming in Week 11, that number was not quite as high. The vast majority of the fans still trust the Dolphins’ direction, but it the losing is clearly having some impact on the confidence. Our Week 11 poll shows a stumble down to 84 percent. What happens if the Dolphins stand toe-to-toe with their division rivals but come up short? How will a loss to the Bills impact next week’s rating? What would an upset win do to the fan confidence? We will be back early next week to ask for your updated confidence in Miami’s direction. title: Miami Dolphins offensive line review: Tracking the guards in Week 10
summary: When you lose a close game to a bad opponent and your quarterback gets strip-sacked for a defensive touchdown, you might assume the offensive line had a terrible afternoon. The reality is more complicated. The Dolphins nearly completed a 14-point comeback but ultimately fell 24-22 to the Colts in Week 10, a game that highlighted […]
full_text: When you lose a close game to a bad opponent and your quarterback gets strip-sacked for a defensive touchdown, you might assume the offensive line had a terrible afternoon. The reality is more complicated. The Dolphins nearly completed a 14-point comeback but ultimately fell 24-22 to the Colts in Week 10, a game that highlighted a seemingly downward trend for the team as a whole. That may be especially true for the offensive line, where rookie left guard Kadyn Proctor and second-year right guard Jonah Savaiinaea remain key pieces of the Dolphins’ future. While the offense struggled as a whole, player development doesn’t stop because of one ugly afternoon, and that’s especially true for two young guards expected to be part of the foundation moving forward. Each week, we take a closer look at Proctor and Savaiinaea and examine what analysts are saying about their most recent performances. Kadyn Proctor Game Snap Counts Penalties PFF Overall Grade PFF Run Blocking PFF Pass Protection 9/13, @ Raiders 59 (100%) 1 71.2 79.0 63.4 9/20, @ 49ers 56 (100%) 2 62.0 72.4 39.1 9/27, vs. Chiefs 73 (100%) 0 57.5 51.1 71.3 10/4, @ Vikings 39 (100%) 0 51.2 48.6 64.9 10/11, vs. Bengals 66 (100%) 0 72.7 74.9 52.2 BYE 10/25, @ Jets 65 (100%) 0 59.6 58.2 61.3 DNP 11/8, vs. Lions 57 (100%) 0 57.3 50.2 72.6 11/15, @ Colts 69 (100%) 0 63.9 55.0 84.3 Jonah Savaiinaea Game Snap Counts Penalties PFF Overall Grade PFF Run Blocking PFF Pass Protection 9/13, @ Raiders 59 (100%) 0 47.6 50.9 38.2 9/20, @ 49ers 56 (100%) 0 65.9 68.5 46.1 9/27, vs. Chiefs 73 (100%) 0 56.6 58.4 47.5 10/4, @ Vikings 39 (100%) 0 49.5 44.6 77.5 10/11, vs. Bengals 18 (27%) 0 45.4 44.7 78.4 BYE 10/25, @ Jets 65 (100%) 0 49.4 53.5 31.4 11/1, vs. Patriots 65 (100%) 1 49.7 51.9 63.4 11/8, vs. Lions 57 (100%) 0 45.8 46.0 44.3 11/15, @ Colts 69 (100%) 0 58.8 64.8 36.3 What We Learned When you think of the ideal offensive line, you’re probably thinking of five guys who have played together for a long time and who understand what the quarterback likes to do in certain game situations. At this moment in time, the Dolphins have none of that. In Week 5, Savaiinaea misses most of the game due to injury. Proctor misses Week 8 while in concussion protocol. Against the Colts, Andrew Meyer played the entire game at center while Aaron Brewer is treated for his own concussion, and the team is led by a brand new quarterback in Kyle McCord. With all of these injuries and new faces, you can’t really be surprised when plays break down and players don’t know where to go. A big reason why the offensive line held up as well as it did – even without Brewer – is Kadyn Proctor. There’s an old line about offensive linemen: Strong o-line performance slips by the average viewer – it’s when you make a mistake that you stand out. Proctor has been steady most of the season, but especially lately: Fewer bad reps as the season moves along, with steady, consistent growth. His PFF grades averages out to a slightly above league-average 61.9, which is remarkable for a rookie, and his pass protection over the past two games is bordering on elite. LockedOn Dolphins’ Kyle Crabbs said this week that Proctor’s last three games “have graded as the three best games that he has played this season.” As for Jonah Savaiinaea, the picture is a little murkier. Crabbs has been increasingly critical of his play since the bye week, arguing in the same video that the Colts game featured several examples of the inconsistency that plagued him as a rookie. One missed block late in the game potentially cost Ollie Gordon a significant gain during Miami’s final drive. That said, PFF ranked his performance against the Colts as his second-best overall and against the pass. Maybe Savaiinaea is just slow to develop (remember how long it took Austin Jackson to turn into a serviceable starter?), and the last month has raised questions about how much of Savaiinaea’s hot start was sustainable. Jonah for sure has more development to do, especially against the pass (PFF grades <45 in 3 of the past 4 games). I still have hope. One last point we touched on before: Perhaps more than anywhere else on the team, offensive line performance is a team effort, especially as opposing defenses become more nuanced and creative. Offensive-line play is often evaluated as if the five linemen operate in isolation. They don’t. A failed run can be traced to a guard losing a block, but it can also be caused by a tight end missing an assignment (cough Dulcich cough), a receiver failing to seal the edge, a protection call that never gets communicated or the absence of an All-Pro center who normally keeps everything organized. Against Indianapolis, we saw examples of all of the above. That’s why a strip-sack, a stuffed run or a pressure allowed doesn’t always tell the full story. When looking at o-line scoring, I try to remember that context matters. The tracker will be updated each week throughout the season. For a more in-depth breakdown of Proctor’s and Savaiinaea’s performance, check out offensive line Coach Eric Smith’s film analysis of the game, which you can find on his YouTube channel, Focused on Fins .

title: 5 Things I Think I Think About the Miami Dolphins After Week 10
summary: If you’re looking for a silver lining after the Miami Dolphins’ 24-22 loss to the Indianapolis Colts, I have good news: The franchise may have found themselves a new hero, and it’s Zane Gonzalez. Here are 5 things I think I think after the head-shaking loss to the Daniel Jones-led Colts. Zane Gonzalez: Miami Dolphins […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FLORIDA - NOVEMBER 08: Derrick Moore #8 of the Detroit Lions rushes Malik Willis #2 of the Miami Dolphins during the first half of the game at Hard Rock Stadium on November 08, 2026 in Miami Gardens, Florida. (Photo by Megan Briggs/Getty Images) | Getty Images If you’re looking for a silver lining after the Miami Dolphins’ 24-22 loss to the Indianapolis Colts, I have good news: The franchise may have found themselves a new hero, and it’s Zane Gonzalez. Here are 5 things I think I think after the head-shaking loss to the Daniel Jones-led Colts. Zane Gonzalez: Miami Dolphins Superfan From the Future It’s February 10, 2030. At Nashville’s Nissan Stadium, the New York Jets just won their first Super Bowl in more than 50 years. Gang Green is celebrating: Champagne, laughter, tears. Three years earlier, the Colts had traded away the pick that became the No. 1 selection in the 2027 draft. Now the quarterback chosen with that pick has delivered New York a championship. In the on-air interview, head coach Aaron Glenn hugs his third-year superstar quarterback, yelling joyously to the cameras, “We’re only here because of this guy! He put us on his back and carried us to become world champions!” The words “world champions” echo in the brain of thirty-four-year-old Miami Subs employee Zane Gonzalez as he shuts off the black-and-white television in his parents’ basement. Zane takes in all the Miami Dolphins gear around his room – his prized foam finger from 1984, the 8-inch T.D. stuffy on his pillow – and sighs. “Where did we go wrong, T.D.?” he asks his stuffy. “How did the Jets win the Super Bowl while we’re still looking for a playoff win?” T.D. stares at him, unblinking. “You’re right, it was that 2027 draft. That win over the Colts knocked us out of the running for the top pick in the draft! We should have been the Super Bowl winners this year!” He looks up. “T.D., I know what I must do.” Six months later, after convincing Dolphins owner Stephen Ross to invest $500 million in temporal engineering, Gonzalez steps into a prototype time machine and travels three years into the past. His mission is simple: Convince the Dolphins to bring him on as placekicker. And then? Miss. Miss against the Patriots. Miss against the Lions. Most importantly: Miss against the Colts. Make sure Miami loses enough games to stay ahead of the Colts in the draft order. Land the future franchise quarterback who would finally deliver the Dolphins’ long-awaited Super Bowl title. Sacrifice a few meaningless wins today and the Dolphins become champions tomorrow. After all, no one would willingly miss two field goals and an extra point in a game his team lost by two … right? It’s January 11, 2027. Zane Gonzalez stands at South Pointe Park Pier, staring out at the Atlantic. The day before, the Dolphins lost to the Patriots, finishing off a 2-15 season and securing the first overall pick in the upcoming draft, one win ahead of the sad sack Colts. “Excuse me. Are you … Zane Gonzalez?” He turns. A little girl, maybe six years old, stands behind him in an oversized Ricky Williams jersey. She clutches her well-loved T.D. stuffed dolphin under one arm. “Yes,” Gonzalez says. “That’s me.” The girl looks him up and down. Then spits at his feet. “Nice kicking, dill weed.” Before he can respond, she pivots and marches away. Gonzalez watches her disappear down the pier. A smile touches the corner of his mouth. He turns back toward the ocean. “You’re welcome,” he whispers after her. A single tear rolls down his cheek. The Defense Continues To Dominate Two weeks ago, the Dolphins held a Drake Maye-led Patriots offense to 3 points in the first half. Last week, that same defense limited Detroit’s high-powered offense to one of its lowest point totals of the season. And while the final score on Sunday will show the Colts scored 20 points, the reality is a little different. After halftime, Indianapolis managed exactly three offensive points. Daniel Jones finished with fewer than 110 passing yards. The Dolphins intercepted him twice, returned one for a touchdown, forced a fumble and repeatedly forced Indianapolis off the field with three-and-outs. By the fourth quarter, the defense was dragging the rest of the team back into the game whether it wanted to come along or not. The usual suspects were everywhere. Chris Johnson (59-yard pick six) continues to look like one of the steals of the draft. Michael Taaffe (6 tackles, 1 pass defended) once again found ways to impact the game. Chop Robinson (1 sack, 2 QB hits) consistently disrupted the pocket. Jordyn Brooks (9 tackles, 1 pass defended) was all over the field. The Dolphins spotted Indianapolis seven points, generated almost nothing in the kicking game, and still found themselves with a chance to win in the final minutes because the defense spent the second half strangling the Colts offense. For a unit that has carried this team for much of the season, it was another outstanding performance. The Injury Bill Finally Came Due Remember this scene from the greatest movie of all time? The Dolphins’ defense is now the Bluesmobile. The Dolphins entered the game without Zach Sieler. Then Jordan Phillips got hurt, and is out for the year. Then Zeek Biggers got hurt, and he’s out for the year. By the end of the afternoon, Miami was essentially down to Kenneth Grant and Keith Cooper as healthy defensive tackles. In-game, that degree of attrition eventually catches up with you. Without those defensive tackles, the run defense clearly felt the strain. Indianapolis finished with 172 rushing yards as Jonathan Taylor and Seth McGowan consistently found running lanes. The Dolphins simply didn’t have their usual flexibility up front – too many snaps played by too few healthy bodies. Miami’s defense was good enough to win Sunday, but it wasn’t healthy enough to win Sunday. Kyle McCord Looked Like a Rookie … and That’s OK Let’s get the obvious part out of the way first: Kyle McCord made mistakes. The strip-sack touchdown changed the game. The late sack in the fourth quarter was costly. Neither play can simply be ignored because he’s a rookie. But: The strip-sack wasn’t the result of panic – it was a quarterback trying to make the correct read and reacting a second too slowly. The late sack wasn’t a quarterback seeing ghosts as much as a young passer processing pressure incorrectly while trying to work deeper into the progression. And then there’s everything else. McCord converted a third-and-13. He made several NFL-caliber throws. He stayed aggressive. And he didn’t fall apart after the strip-sack touchdown put seven points on the board for Indianapolis. Young quarterbacks have gotten rattled by far less. Instead, McCord kept battling and gave Miami a chance to win. If you’re looking for reasons to be optimistic, Sunday’s mistakes looked fixable. The End Is Near, and So We Face the Final Curtain Back in August, I was so young and naïve, blinded by optimism that 2026 would lead to a glorious 6-11 season. Sure, we’re rebuilding, but at least as the youngest team in the league, we would avoid some of those devastating injuries the league’s more geriatric squads had to deal with. Now? Now we have Kyle McCord handing the ball off to Ollie Gordon behind a leakier-than-expected offensive line. Our defensive tackles are so decimated, that we’re down to three starters – Kenneth Grant, Keith Cooper and you, dear reader. Go suit up. The team is still in evaluation mode, and there’s still a lot of meaningful development that can and should happen for our first- and second-year starters. But the pipe dream of 6 wins feels especially unattainable now. At 38%, the Dolphins have the best odds to pick first in the 2027 draft, according to the prediction market platform Kalshi. ESPN gives the team a 41% chance, also first. I’d like to see the Dolphins win against the Jets the Sunday after Thanksgiving. A two-win season isn’t great, but if both wins come against the Jets, that can…

Miami signed punter Jack Browning to the practice squad this week and is expected to elevate him to the […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MN - OCTOBER 04: Miami Dolphins center Aaron Brewer (55) looks on during the NFL game between the Miami Dolphins and the Minnesota Vikings on October 4th, 2026, at U.S. Bank Stadium in Minneapolis, MN. (Photo by Bailey Hillesheim/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Miami Dolphins will be without punter Bradley Pinoin on Sunday as they face the Buffalo Bills. Pinion has a right groin injury and missed practice all week before being ruled out on Friday’s injury report. Miami signed punter Jack Browning to the practice squad this week and is expected to elevate him to the active roster by today’s 4 p.m. Eastern deadline. The Dolphins are also making a change at kicker this week, waiving Zane Gonzalez after he missed three kicks last week and signing kicker Daniel Carlson to the practice squad. Long snapper Tucker Addington is the lone specialist on the roster and the only one of the three who has played a game for Miami prior to this weekend’s contest. Miami also ruled out wide receiver Jared Wayne for Sunday’s game. He has a quadriceps injury. The Dolphins injury report included cornerback Jaylin Simpson (knee) and safety Dante Trader Jr. (shoulder/groin), both doubtful for the game. Cornerback Darrell Baker Jr. (knee), center Aaron Brewer (concussion), and cornerback Marcellas Dial Jr. (toe) are all questionable. Brewer, who missed last week’s game with the head injury, fully participated in practice on Friday and, as long as he has no symptoms on Saturday, should be cleared to play. The Bills side of the reports includes cornerback Christian Benford (groin) and linebacker Dorian Williams (calf) having been ruled out of the game while tight end Dalton Kincaid (thumb/ankle) is doubtful. Safety Damar Hamlin (toe), defensive tackle T.J. Sanders (defensive tackle), and tight end Jackson Hawes (shoulder) are all questionable. Dolphins offensive coordinator analyzes QB Kyle McCord; will Dolphins spy Josh Allen? – Chris Perkins, South Florida Sun Sentinel Dolphins quarterback Kyle McCord played better after his third quarter strip-sack fumble that resulted in a touchdown for the Indianapolis Colts in last week’s 24-22 loss, according to offensive coordinator Bobby Slowik. title: Daniel Jones has been released by the Colts. Should the Patriots go after him?
summary: You heard about a Friday news dump, but have you heard about a Friday QB dump? That’s precisely what the Indianapolis Colts did when they released their starting quarterback, Daniel Jones, earlier today. Jones, 29, was in his second season with the franchise and just eight months removed from signing a two-year, $88 million contract […]
full_text: You heard about a Friday news dump, but have you heard about a Friday QB dump? That’s precisely what the Indianapolis Colts did when they released their starting quarterback , Daniel Jones, earlier today. Jones, 29, was in his second season with the franchise and just eight months removed from signing a two-year, $88 million contract extension. However, he and the Colts as a whole have struggled mightily this year, leading to some sweeping changes within the organization. First, they fired the GM who signed him to that deal, Chris Ballard, and now they let go of Jones himself. His release comes with the Colts at 3-8 and Jones having completed 205 of 351 pass attempts (58.4%) for 1,974 yards with seven touchdowns and 13 interceptions. A year removed from tearing his Achilles tendon, he is ranked 30th among 31 qualifying quarterbacks in EPA per play this season (-0.139) and 31st in both net yards per attempt (4.8) and completion percentage above expectation (-6.1). Long story short, he has been dreadful. And yet, the New England Patriots might just keep a close eye on him. The Patriots, after all, saw their own starting QB, Drake Maye, suffer a fractured fibula during last Sunday’s loss versus the Detroit Lions. While it remains to be seen how long he will be out, Maye missing most if not all of his team’s seven final regular season games this year would not come as a surprise. The question now becomes whether or not the Patriots should pursue Jones as a replacement. Let’s make the argument in favor of and against such a move. Why the Patriots should sign Daniel Jones Before making this argument, it needs to be prefaced with this: everything in this section only applies to Jones going through the waiver wire unclaimed and making it to the open market. According to Jason Fitzgerald of Over the Cap, a team would need $6.35 million in salary cap space to claim Jones — financial flexibility the Patriots do not have at the moment. If he passes waivers, he could be signed to a deal worth as little as $505,554. With that out of the way, let’s take a look at why brining Jones in would make sense for the Patriots. It all starts with one question: would he be an upgrade over Tommy DeVito for however long Drake Maye will be sidelined? His play this season so far suggests that that might not be the case. However, a change in environment might help Jones regain some of the confidence he had in his first year with the Colts, when he played some of the best football of his career and finished the season sixth in the league in EPA per play (0.201). If the Patriots can get a fraction of that, they should be happy with Jones as a better alternative than DeVito. In addition, Jones also has some familiarity with the Patriots scheme. While he never played directly under offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels, he did spend the better part of three seasons under former New England assistant Brian Daboll. The offense Daboll ran with the Giants has similarities to McDaniels’ in terms of terminology, quarterback responsibility and play designs, meaning that the lead-up time for Jones to get ready would be comparatively small. Inserting Jones would likely also not come with significant philosophical changes. In essence, after all, he is a similar player type as Maye is: somebody capable of making plays with his arm as well as his legs, as evidenced by his career rushing average of 6.1 yards per carry. While his highs have not been close to Maye’s, he has shown that he can be an adequate NFL starting quarterback and somebody able to elevate the talent around him. That obviously was not the case in Indianapolis this season, but if a change of scenery and move to a better-run team can get him close to that, it would be precisely what the Patriots need right now if there are any doubts about DeVito. And even if not, what do the Patriots have to lose? They are 5-5 and fighting for their playoff lives, and signing Jones would not automatically disqualify them from starting DeVito. At the very least, he would provide veteran depth better suited to challenge the post-Maye hierarchy than sixth-round rookie Behren Morton. Why the Patriots shouldn’t sign Daniel Jones On Friday, Jones became the first quarterback in the NFL in more than three decades to get released less than 24 hours after starting a game. That plus the fact the Colts are willing to cut their losses despite the financial investment they made in him just this offseason should tell you all you need to know. It’s been bad this year. Very, very bad. While there might be a snowballing effect to Jones’ struggles and a fresh start could indeed help him regain the form he previously showed, there is no denying he has played some of the worst football in the NFL this year. The numbers mentioned above are an illustration of that. Some of it had to do with the surroundings and a Colts team that a) lacking quality across the board, and b) is in a free fall since October. In addition, his injury situation also seems to have played a part in it: 12 months after his torn Achilles, he still does not look like he is close to 100% and fails to consistently to step into throws, maneuver the pocket and pick up yards on the ground, averaging just 3.8 yards per carry. On top of it, Jones has been a streaky player throughout his career. While there have been stretches of play where he lived up to his former first-round status, the lows have been underwhelming, including this season. Given all of that, expecting a quick turnaround in New England would be naive, particularly considering that the Patriots are missing several offensive pieces because of injury. But even if they didn’t, Jones would not have any familiarity with them: despite some experience in a McDaniels-style system, he would have to build chemistry with his receiving corps, offensive line and coaching staff on the fly. Tommy DeVito, meanwhile, has a two-year head start in that regard. Speaking of DeVito, he was signed to a contract extension in the offseason to serve as QB2 and has, by all accounts, been a model citizen deserving of his shot. Obviously, the job should go to the best option regardless of contract situation. That said, all things considered — including what a change might mean for the locker room — DeVito still has a strong case to be just that. Verdict Even though they are still in a competitive position on paper, the Patriots are fighting for their playoff lives with Drake Maye sidelined for the foreseeable future. Their margin for error, meanwhile, is, to quote safety Kevin Byard, “basically at zero.” Would adding Jones increase it and allow New England to play winning football during Maye’s absence? Ideally, that is not a question they would have to ask; Tommy DeVito stepping in and leading the offense at an adequate level would be the best-case scenario. Of course, as the Lions game showed, there is a realistic chance the lights are too bright for him. The problem is, they also might be for Jones. So far this season, after all, he has not been good and not been able to hold up to the pressure of being the guy at quarterback in Indianapolis. He wouldn’t quite be that in New England, sure, but the eyes of one of the NFL’s biggest markets would still be on him. Would that prevent the Patriots from signing him? Probably not. Still, it is one of the factors to consider alongside the arguments outlined above. And putting all of those together, it is clear the decision whether or not to sign Jones as a potential stand-in for Maye is quite nuanced. At the end of the day, Mike Vrabel, Eliot Wolf and Ryan Cowden — the latter of whom spent time with Jones in New York — will have to see their way through it. And once they do, they very well might find that the potential disruption caused by adding Jones might not be worth the theoretical gains. What do you think about Daniel Jones? Should the Patriots pursue him, or steer clear of him? Please head down to the comment…

summary: The Saints are coming into a matchup on Sunday where the defense will face one of its toughest opponents. The Bears will come in looking to expose some of the biggest holes on the team. full_text: KNOXVILLE, TENNESSEE - SEPTEMBER 26: Xavier Gilliam #2 of the Tennessee Volunteers pressures Arch Manning #16 of the Texas Longhorns during a game between the Tennessee Volunteers and the Texas Longhorns at Neyland Stadium on September 26, 2026 in Knoxville, Tennessee. (Photo by Roger Wimmer/ISI Photos/ISI Photos via Getty Images) | ISI Photos via Getty Images The Saints are coming into a matchup on Sunday where the defense will face one of its toughest opponents. The Bears will come in looking to expose some of the biggest holes on the team. Here are some college players to watch who can help fill those holes. Interior defensive tackle is the biggest need for this team. At 2:30 PM on ABC, LSU will be taking on one of the best in Xavier Gilliam. So far this season, Gilliam has 6 sacks and 33 pressures from the interior, along with 11.5 TFLs. That’s something the Saints could use right now. We have spoken about Will Echoles several times, and Ole Miss will be playing against Wofford at 11 AM on SECN+, but there is another DT who needs to receive more attention, and that’s David Stone. Stone is a force in the middle for the Oklahoma Sooners, and they will be playing Texas A&M at 2:45 PM on ESPN2. So far this season, Stone has 36 tackles and 3 sacks. Of course, a true lockdown corner would be a treat for the Saints, but they currently hold the 11th position in the draft. If the season keeps going the way it is, they may find themselves in a more favorable spot to draft the No. 1 overall cornerback in the draft, and that’s Notre Dame’s Leonard Moore. Moore will be playing against SMU at 6:30 PM on NBC. Through 8 games, Moore has 19 tackles. He has an opponent completion percentage of 42% and has allowed only 112 receiving yards the entire season. There’s also Ashton Hampton. Hampton is considered one of the best corners in this draft as well, and he and the Clemson Tigers will be playing Duke on Friday at 6:30 PM on ESPN. So far this season, Hampton has 2 interceptions and 45 tackles. Both corners have great size, speed, and ball skills. Finally, the Saints have to take a look at adding a safety if there isn’t a cornerback or defensive tackle available. There will be a good group to select from. Brauntae Johnson plays with Leonard Moore at Notre Dame. Johnson is a 6’2″ safety who can cover in the slot as well as play deep. Another safety to watch out for is Jelani McDonald at Texas. McDonald and the Longhorns will be playing against Arkansas at 2:30 PM on ESPN. McDonald just had one of the best games a safety could have, recording 3 INTs against LSU in Death Valley, giving him 4 on the year. The 6’2″, 201-pound safety possesses excellent size and range to play in a secondary alongside Jonas Sanker. Who are some other players you will have your eyes on this weekend? title: Saints vs. Bears: Key Matchups
summary: The New Orleans Saints are walking into Chicago as double-digit underdogs against the Bears. The Saints have dropped two of their last three, and their season has quickly been derailed. Now in desperate need of a win, New Orleans will face their former head coach and current Bears defensive coordinator, Dennis Allen, in a game […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LA - NOVEMBER 15: Travis Etienne Jr. #3 of the New Orleans Saints warms up before a game against the Carolina Panthers at Caesars Superdome on November 15, 2026, in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Derick Hingle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New Orleans Saints are walking into Chicago as double-digit underdogs against the Bears. The Saints have dropped two of their last three, and their season has quickly been derailed. Now in desperate need of a win, New Orleans will face their former head coach and current Bears defensive coordinator, Dennis Allen, in a game they were completely outmatched in just a year ago. If the Saints want to steal a win, it will be by taking advantage of these key matchups. QB Tyler Shough vs. Bears pass rush Saints fans will be the first ones to tell you about Allen’s capabilities as a defensive playcaller. The former Saints head coach was known for his ability to call up exotic looks at the line of scrimmage, something that has become even more relevant this season with the massive success of Brian Flores and the Minnesota Vikings defense. Tyler Shough has been a bright spot for the Saints this season, but is coming off one of the more disappointing games of his career. Even worse for Shough and the Saints, this was against a lackluster Carolina Panthers defense. Now New Orleans will be facing a team that is top-10 in sacks and just made a massive trade for one of the best defensive linemen of the decade, Jeffrey Simmons. The Saints have worked on getting the ball out faster, and it’s improved over the weeks. But pass protection remains a major concern, and with a switch at center, right guard, and right tackle, the Saints could be in for a long day. Saints running backs vs. the Bears’ run defense I don’t think I even have to elaborate here. The Saints are a bottom-five rushing offense in the league, and are coming off a game where running backs averaged 1.5 yards per carry against one of the league’s worst run defenses in the league. Now New Orleans will be facing a team that is top-five against the run. Getting the run started has been a problem all season, and really, it’s more of a Kellen Moore issue than it is a running backs issue. But if the Saints are going to have any chance at keeping up with Chicago’s high-powered offense, it will be by controlling the game on the ground. Saints pass rush vs. QB Caleb Williams The Saints have two of the most dangerous pass rushers this season, with Carl Granderson logging 8.5 sacks and Chase Young getting 8 of his own. Fortunately for the Saints, they’ll be facing a quarterback who holds on to the ball the longest in the NFL. Unfortunately for New Orleans, Caleb Williams’ time from getting the ball and releasing it hasn’t translated into sacks. Over the last two games, Williams has been sacked just twice and has become a playmaker in the face of the pass rush. The former first overall pick’s stats haven’t looked great this season, throwing just 8 touchdowns to 5 interceptions, but he has grown into a leader and can command an offense with the best of them. If the Saints want a chance at winning this game, they’ll likely have to take down the star quarterback three or more times and create impossible goal-to-go situations.

title: Interview with the Enemy: Chicago Bears
summary: This week, the New Orleans Saints will head to Solider Field to face the Chicago Bears in Week 11 of the 2026 regular season. To break it down, Bill Zimmerman of Windy City Gridiron joins us to preview this weekend’s matchup. NJ: How legitimate are the Bears’ Super Bowl aspirations at this point in the […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 19: D'Andre Swift #4 of the Chicago Bears carries the ball against the New Orleans Saints during the second half of the game at Soldier Field on October 19, 2025 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images This week, the New Orleans Saints will head to Solider Field to face the Chicago Bears in Week 11 of the 2026 regular season. To break it down, Bill Zimmerman of Windy City Gridiron joins us to preview this weekend’s matchup. NJ: How legitimate are the Bears’ Super Bowl aspirations at this point in the season? Does it feel like this could finally be the year Chicago gets it done? BZ: The Jeffery Simmons trade changed everything as far as I’m concerned. The Bears defense was the reason they weren’t a true Super Bowl contender. Dennis Allen was largely doing it with smoke and mirrors. Yes, he had really effective blitz packages on 3 rd down, but that wasn’t sustainable in the playoffs against great teams. The offense was never a question; the defense was. With Simmons, he’s a multiplier. In just two games, we’ve seen the play improve of every defensive lineman and linebacker around him. If their front 7 can play like this, it will help a banged-up secondary that is the weakest part of the team. No one can guarantee a Super Bowl, but I do think the Bears are on the short list of true Super Bowl contenders this year (and that’s very foreign to write). NJ: Who are some notable names who will be sidelined for the Bears on Sunday against the Saints? Is there a particular area in which New Orleans could exploit? BZ: The Bears are the healthiest they’ve been in a while heading into this game. They have RB Kyle Monangai returning, which will be a huge boost for their running game, and rookie CB Malik Muhammad may not be the biggest name, but he is a key starter in their secondary. TE Cole Kmet is out for the year, and S Coby Bryant has been out since training camp. The only other notable starter who will be out is CB Kyler Gordon, who injured his shoulder against Tampa; he did finish the game, but he is now listed as out for this one. The key to stopping the Bears is to attack their cornerbacks. It’s the weakest part of the roster, but you have to make sure you are getting the ball out quickly before Jeffery Simmons collapses the pocket. NJ: How much of an impact has Dennis Allen had on turning around the Bears’ defense throughout his tenure? Have there been any decisions or coaching tendencies that have rubbed fans the wrong way? BZ: I think Dennis Allen is very popular among Bears fans, and I think he was the perfect DC hire with Ben Johnson. I think Dennis Allen is at a point where he almost certainly isn’t going to get another head coaching job. That means he should be able to pair with Johnson and be the top coaches on this coaching staff for years to come. If things go well, they’ll have an Andy Reid/Steve Spagnuolo type partnership. I think, before the Simmons trade, people had been frustrated with how Dennis Allen wanted to build his defensive line, but other than that, I think Bears fans are very happy with how he calls a game, and I think most of us understand that he got a lot more success out of his defense than the level of talent that was on the field. The best thing he’s done in Chicago is create a phenomenal third down defense. The Bears have been quite strong on third downs and it’s forcing teams to get big chunk plays on the early downs or end up punting the ball back to the Bears. NJ: Who is one Bears player you think Saints fans should keep an eye on Sunday—someone who may not receive much national attention but could have a strong performance? BZ: Offensively, I don’t think there are many names to give because Caleb Williams, Luther Burden, Colston Loveland, and Rome Odunze are their main weapons, and I think football fans are pretty familiar with all of them. I do think Kyle Monangai is going to be a big part of the offensive game plan and split carries with D’Andre Swift so Monangai is one returning from injury that I think can have a strong game. Defensively, I mentioned Muhammad, but I’ll give you Austin Booker. He was a 5th-round pick in 2024 out of Missouri, and he’s been coming into his own this year as an improved run defender and a solid pass rusher. You should hear Booker’s name at least once on Sunday, either making a TFL or a sack. NJ: According to FanDuel Sportsbook , the Bears (-720) are currently 11.5-point favorites over the Saints (+520) in Sunday’s matchup; what is your final score prediction and how do you see the game playing out? BZ: It’s really hard to imagine that the Bears don’t win this one. Ben Johnson is great on extra rest, and the Bears are healthy, and I don’t think it’s an insult to say the Bears are simply a better team than the Saints and are playing them at home. I think the question isn’t who will win or whether the Bears cover the big spread? I think the offense is going to have success regardless. I think it comes down to if you think the Saints can get points on the Bears’ defense. If you do, then there’s no reason to think this one couldn’t be like 31 to 21 or so, and the Saints cover. Personally, I do think the Saints will struggle on offense against the Bears, and I think the Bears will win this one comfortably by 2 or 3 scores. I’ll call it 31 to 13. Thank you again to Bill Zimmerman for joining us to preview this week’s matchup! You can check out the rest of his work here .

title: College Football Week 12: Three draft prospects to watch for the NY Giants
summary: Good morning New York Giants fans! Happy Saturday and welcome to Week 12 of the college football season. The college football playoff picture is starting to come into focus, and we’re seeing some truly surprising teams enter the Top 12. Much as we didn’t expect Indiana or Miami to make the runs they did last […]
full_text: ﻿UCLA running back Wayne Knight carries the ball | ISI Photos via Getty Images Good morning New York Giants fans! Happy Saturday and welcome to Week 12 of the college football season. The college football playoff picture is starting to come into focus, and we’re seeing some truly surprising teams enter the Top 12. Much as we didn’t expect Indiana or Miami to make the runs they did last year, so too have teams like Utah, Wake Forest, and UCLA surprised us. As usual, we’re using the NFL Draft as a lens through which to look at both college football and the state of the Giants. We’ll be spotlighting players who could fill potential needs on the Giants’ roster come draft time — and today that’s wide receiver, running back, and cornerback. Georgia Tech vs. (11) Wake Forest ESPN – noon Player spotlight: Carlos Hernandez (WR, Wake Forest) No, that isn’t a typo, the Demon Decons are 11th in the country and should make the College Football Playoffs. And one of the biggest engines driving their rise up the rankings has been wide receiver Carlos Hernandez. The 6-foot, 190 pound senior has emerged as one of the most prolific wideouts in the country. So far this year he’s hauled in 67 catches for 1,039 yards, and 8 touchdowns. Hernandez might not have blazing speed, but he’s a detailed route runner who has excellent start-stop quickness and explosiveness out of his breaks. He reminds of Victor Cruz with a thick lower body, great contact balance, and a tendency to turn into a running back after making the catch. It’s easy to see him turning into an instant star in the right situation. Michigan vs. (4) UCLA CBS – 3:30 p.m. Player spotlight: Wayne Knight (RB, UCLA) I wouldn’t blame anyone for watching the game between Tennessee and LSU instead of this one, but I also didn’t want to wait longer to spotlight UCLA running back Wayne Knight. Knight isn’t getting the national attention of backs like Jadan Baugh or Kewan Lacey, but he has been one of the country’s best runners since QB Nico Iamaleava was lost for the season. Knight is a compact sparkplug of a back at 5-foot-7, 200 pounds with great vision and patience behind the line of scrimmage to go with his natural leverage, quickness, and contact balance. He excels at pressing his blocks, using his size to hide behind offensive linemen, then exploding through holes to pick up yardage. His short legs not only make him hard to tackle, but also give him great stride frequency that make for great acceleration and quickness. And while he might not look it, Knight is both a tenacious short-yardage back and fast enough to outrun the athletic Oregon defense. (21) South Carolina vs. (1) Georgia ABC – 7:30 p.m. Player spotlight: Vicari Swain (CB, South Carolina) Sitting here, I believe that the Giants should extend Deonte Banks, at least locking up their starting corners for the next few seasons. And while the Giants just drafted Colton Hood out of Tennessee, they could look to draft another in the first two days to maintain their depth at the position if they move on from Paulson Adebo. Swain is a classic “South Carolina” corner with solid size (6-foot, 195 pounds), fluid hips, a physical demeanor, and the upside to be a sticky press-man corner. He also has a good nose for the ball with 9 passes defensed, 3 interceptions, and 2 forced fumbles over the last two seasons. All of that fits well in Dennard Wilson’s defense. But what could really put him over the top in the eyes of John Harbaugh is his special teams upside. Swain serves as one of South Carolina’s primary punt returners and currently leads the SEC in punt return yardage. He’s averaged 14.4 yards per return over the last two years and has 5 punt return touchdowns since the start of last season. He led the SEC in return touchdowns last year with 3 and currently leads the conference with 2 return touchdowns. Returner has been a revolving door for the Giants, and finding a reserve corner, with starting upside, who is also a potential weapon as a returner could be very attractive.
