title: Should the Seahawks hold Quenton Nelson out of the 49ers game?
summary: Arguably, the biggest trade deadline acquisition of the 2026 season came when the Seattle Seahawks enticed the Indianapolis Colts to part with their All-World and likely future Hall of Fame LG Quenton Nelson for the measly sum of a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-rounder. This move was supposed to be a shot in […]
full_text: Arguably, the biggest trade deadline acquisition of the 2026 season came when the Seattle Seahawks enticed the Indianapolis Colts to part with their All-World and likely future Hall of Fame LG Quenton Nelson for the measly sum of a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-rounder . This move was supposed to be a shot in the arm for both the pass and run game, and was likely not just a rental even though Nelson is in the final year of his contract. Moving last year’s first-round pick Grey Zabel over to RG is a clear sign that Seattle views that lineup as the ideal long term scenario to build a studly OL. Unfortunately, this new lineup lasted just one game, a rare home Monday Night Football loss to the Chicago Bears 34-17. It was one of the worst games I’ve seen the Seahawks play under Mike Macdonald, and a big part of that was the offensive line struggles. Sam Darnold was sacked three times, once by new Chicago Bear Jeffrey Simmons who was a problem all night. Zabel’s struggles at RG threw some cold water on the plan. I figured there would be growing pains, so it wasn’t necessarily a surprise. The theory is that the new lineup would be able to gel over the following two games against the Arizona Cardinals and Las Vegas Raiders, head into the bye feeling good, and be ready for the stretch run. A sound idea, but during the week following the Bears debacle, it was announced that Nelson had aggravated a previous knee injury that he had with the Colts and needed a procedure. As I write this, Seattle is on its bye and Macdonald has characterized Nelson as “week-to-week” stating that if they had practice over the bye, Nelson would likely not be participating. Seattle’s next game is a huge division matchup in San Francisco, one they need to win to have any hope left to win the NFC West, no matter how slim the chances are. Nelson might not even be healthy enough to play, but even if he is, should the coaching staff hold him off for another week? That probably sounds like a really dumb idea and I should be tarred and feathered for even positing that question. The Seahawks traded draft capital for Nelson, he’s one of the best guards in the NFL, and they need to decide whether or not he should be extended. Plus, every game he sits out would mean just postponing the inevitability of Zabel moving back to RG. Believe me, I get all of that. Yet, maybe it’s not so bad to shift that scenario back another week? Seattle’s rushing attack has been better of late, with 150 yards or more in two of the last four games and 120+ in three of four, with the only stinker coming against Chicago…when Nelson was playing LG and Zabel at RG. Charles Cross will hopefully be back in the lineup, but backup Josh Jones might need to play RT since Abraham Lucas injured his ankle against the Raiders. Bringing Nelson back would put the starting LT and LG for the last two games at RT and RG. That kind of sounds like a disaster waiting to happen, particularly against a strong San Francisco defense. When the Seahawks lost to the 49ers in Week 5, they gave up five sacks and turned the ball over 4 times which led directly to 21 points for San Francisco. The starting OL featured Cross, Zabel, Jalen Sundell, a platoon of Christian Haynes/Beau Stephens, and Abraham Lucas. And still Seattle arguably should have won. In this important rematch, swapping Anthony Bradford and Jones in at RG and RT couldn’t perform worse than the Week 5 OL did (knock on wood). I don’t think I’d feel as confident saying that with the projected lineup if Nelson returns given the results against Chicago. Maybe letting Nelson get another week under his belt in the system wouldn’t be such a bad thing? Seattle would have the best chance short-term to get a victory in Santa Clara. Long-term, insert Nelson into the lineup for the rest of the season and work out the kinks against the ¾ of the NFC East (Dallas Cowboys, New York Giants, and Philadelphia Eagles) before the two matchups against the Los Angeles Rams. That idea might sound counterintuitive, but it could give Seattle the best chance to win as many games as possible, a necessity if they want to make the playoffs. Survive, advance, and play your best ball at the end of the season. Holding Nelson out until after the 49ers game could be the best way to achieve all of those goals and keep their dreams alive.
author: Ted Zahn

title: Seahawks Reacts survey results: Fans split on starting Sam Darnold over Drew Lock
summary: The Seattle Seahawks have a big decision to make at quarterback heading into their Week 12 matchup against the San Francisco 49ers. With Sam Darnold and Drew Lock both in the conversation, Seahawks fans are nearly evenly split on who should get the start. Who should start at QB against the 49ers? Sam Darnold received […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks have a big decision to make at quarterback heading into their Week 12 matchup against the San Francisco 49ers. With Sam Darnold and Drew Lock both in the conversation, Seahawks fans are nearly evenly split on who should get the start. Who should start at QB against the 49ers? Sam Darnold received 52% of the vote, narrowly edging out Drew Lock, who finished with 48%. The results reflect just how divided the fanbase is over Seattle’s quarterback situation, despite the significant statistical gap between the two signal-callers. Lock has arguably made the most of his opportunities this season. In four appearances, including three starts, he has completed 73.1% of his passes for 837 yards, seven touchdowns and no interceptions. His 125.6 passer rating is considerably higher than Darnold’s 79.5. Darnold, meanwhile, has thrown for 1,478 yards and 10 touchdowns in seven games, but also has nine interceptions while completing just 60.2% of his passes. However, the numbers don’t tell the entire story. Darnold has faced a considerably tougher schedule, going up against four of the NFL’s top 11 scoring defenses. Lock, on the other hand, has benefited from matchups against the Cardinals and Raiders, who are tied for allowing the most points per game in the league. That context makes the debate more interesting. Lock has been more efficient and has taken better care of the football, but his performances have come against significantly weaker opposition. Darnold has struggled with turnovers, yet has faced a much tougher test throughout his starts. With Seattle preparing for another divisional showdown against San Francisco, it’s no surprise that fans remain split on who gives the team the best chance to win. Here are some of your comments! The second question focused on the broader direction of the franchise, and the results were considerably less divided. Are you confident the Seahawks are headed in the right direction? Despite the uncertainty surrounding the quarterback position, 74% of Seahawks fans remain confident that the team is headed in the right direction. That’s a strong indication that, even with questions still hanging over the offense, most of the fanbase continues to believe in the overall direction of the franchise. Mike Macdonald has already made his stance clear: Sam Darnold remains Seattle’s starting quarterback when healthy. The head coach reiterated that position this week, praising Drew Lock’s performances while emphasizing his belief in what Darnold can bring to the offense. That makes the upcoming decision particularly important, as Seattle needs to establish some stability at the position heading into the second half of the season. The stakes are also getting higher. Seattle is currently in the Wild Card picture, tied with the Rams at 6-4, while still holding an outside chance of catching San Francisco in the NFC West. With the 49ers sitting at 8-1, however, the upcoming divisional matchup carries significant weight. The Seahawks can’t afford to let uncertainty at quarterback become a recurring issue as they try to keep their playoff hopes alive. Ideally, this is a decision Seattle gets right now and doesn’t have to revisit. If the quarterback debate resurfaces later in the season, it could mean the Seahawks have reached a point where their playoff chances are already considerably slimmer, leaving very little room for another adjustment. For a team still fighting for a postseason spot, finding the right answer at quarterback now could make all the difference. The contrast between the two survey results is worth noting: Seahawks fans might not agree on who should lead the offense against San Francisco, but a clear majority still believes the organization is moving in the right direction. What do you think, Seahawks fans? Should Sam Darnold or Drew Lock start against the 49ers? And are you confident Seattle is headed in the right direction? Let us know in the comments! title: Drew Lock or Sam Darnold: Who gives the Seahawks the best chance to win?
summary: The Seattle Seahawks enter their bye week facing a decision that could define the rest of their season. Sam Darnold is expected to return from injury, but Drew Lock has done more than enough to make the quarterback conversation interesting. Lock is 3-0 in games he has started and has appeared in four victories this […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks enter their bye week facing a decision that could define the rest of their season. Sam Darnold is expected to return from injury , but Drew Lock has done more than enough to make the quarterback conversation interesting. Lock is 3-0 in games he has started and has appeared in four victories this season. Across those appearances, he has completed 68 of 93 passes (73.1%) for 837 yards, seven touchdowns and zero interceptions. He has also posted a 125.6 passer rating. Darnold, meanwhile, is 2-4 in his six full starts, with 1,478 passing yards, 10 touchdowns, nine interceptions and a 79.5 passer rating. The numbers make a compelling case for Lock. But there is more to this discussion than the stat sheet. The quality of the defenses they faced, the support provided by the running game and, perhaps most importantly, the type of football Brian Fleury wants his offense to play all matter. The numbers favor Drew Lock, but context matters There is no denying that Lock has been efficient. His 73.1% completion rate, seven touchdowns and zero interceptions are impressive, especially considering he has taken five sacks for 31 yards lost. His 125.6 passer rating is also considerably higher than Darnold’s 79.5. Darnold, on the other hand, has struggled to protect the football. Nine interceptions in six full starts is a significant problem, particularly for a team that wants to build its identity around a strong defense. He has also taken 17 sacks, losing 113 yards in the process. Lock has been more efficient, more careful with the football, and better at avoiding negative plays. Still, the sample size is considerably smaller, and the circumstances surrounding their performances have been very different. The quality of competition matters The biggest argument in Darnold’s favor is the quality of the defenses he has faced. Lock’s four appearances came against the Patriots, Cardinals twice, and Raiders. Arizona and Las Vegas have been among the league’s worst scoring defenses, while New England has been closer to the middle of the pack. Darnold, meanwhile, had a much tougher stretch. His six full starts came against Washington, the Chargers, 49ers, Broncos, Chiefs, and Bears. San Francisco, Denver, Kansas City and Chicago have all presented considerably more difficult defensive challenges than the Cardinals and Raiders. That is a meaningful difference. Lock has taken advantage of favorable matchups, while Darnold has had to deal with considerably tougher defenses. This doesn’t mean Lock’s production should be dismissed. He can only play the teams on Seattle’s schedule, and he has consistently given the Seahawks a chance to win. But comparing their raw numbers without considering the quality of the defenses they faced would be unfair. The running game hasn’t provided the same support One of the biggest differences between the two quarterbacks has been the support they have received from the running game. During Drew Lock’s four victories, Seattle’s running backs (excluding quarterback rushing) produced 472 yards on the ground, averaging 118 yards per game and 4.2 yards per carry. They also scored four touchdowns. During Sam Darnold’s four losses, the running backs managed just 260 yards, averaging 65 yards per game and 3.2 yards per carry. They scored only two touchdowns. That’s a substantial difference. Lock has benefited from a ground game that has been more productive, allowing Seattle to control the pace, stay ahead of the chains and avoid putting too much pressure on its quarterback. But the quality of the defenses they faced makes this comparison even more interesting. Darnold faced run defenses that ranked, on average something near to the 12th in the NFL. His six opponents ranked second, seventh, 10th, 13th, 19th and 24th against the run. Lock’s four opponents, meanwhile, ranked an average of 25th. Their run defenses ranked 14th, 28th, 28th and 31st. In other words, Darnold faced considerably tougher run defenses and still had to deal with a running game that averaged just 65 yards per game in his four losses. Lock had a much more favorable set of matchups and received significantly better production from his running backs. Against Washington, he threw for 379 yards and four touchdowns, while the running backs combined for just 39 yards on 17 carries. He wasn’t the reason Seattle’s offense struggled in that game. He was practically the entire offense. Ultimately, the running game has been a major advantage during Lock’s victories and a significant weakness during Darnold’s losses. That context should be part of any fair evaluation of their performances. Lock’s conservative approach might fit Fleury’s offense better This might be the most important argument in favor of giving Lock the starting job. Darnold probably has a higher ceiling. When everything clicks, he can make throws and create plays that Lock might not be capable of consistently reproducing. His best football is probably better than Lock’s best football. But the other side of that argument is just as important: Darnold’s worst performances can be considerably more damaging than Lock’s. Turnovers have been a recurring problem throughout Darnold’s career. Even during his strong stretches last season, there were moments when questionable decisions threatened to undo the good things he was doing. This season, that tendency has become increasingly difficult to ignore. Lock, at least in this current season, has played a more conservative brand of football. He has taken what defenses give him, avoided forcing throws into coverage and allowed the rest of the team to do its job. That approach could be a better fit for what Brian Fleury is trying to build offensively, especially with a defense capable of keeping games competitive. The Seahawks don’t necessarily need their quarterback to win games by himself. They need someone who can avoid putting the defense in difficult situations, protect the football and take advantage of scoring opportunities. Lock has done exactly that so far. I don’t know if Lock has the talent to win the games Darnold has lost. But Darnold’s turnovers have probably made some of the games Seattle won much more difficult than they needed to be. That is an important part of this discussion, too. This decision could define Seattle’s season There is another important consideration: Seattle might not have the luxury of changing quarterbacks again. At 6-4, the Seahawks are approaching a critical stretch of their season. Their next game against the San Francisco 49ers could determine whether they remain in contention for the NFC West title. More importantly, every loss from this point forward could seriously jeopardize their chances of making the playoffs. That’s why whoever starts against San Francisco will probably remain the starter for the rest of the season, or at least for as long as Seattle still has a realistic path to the postseason. If the Seahawks find themselves needing to change quarterbacks again after that game, it will probably mean they have already lost more games and put their playoff hopes in great danger. There would be little point in continuing to experiment with the position at that stage. This is ultimately what makes the decision so important for Mike Macdonald during the bye week. He isn’t choosing a quarterback for one game. He may be choosing the player who will lead Seattle through the most important stretch of its season. Macdonald has publicly maintained that Darnold remains the team’s starting quarterback when healthy. That suggests he is still the preferred option, and it is entirely possible that his health, rather than a decision to bench him, will determine who starts against San Francisco. But Lock has made this decision much less straightforward. Seattle doesn’t necessarily need someone capable of making spectacular plays every week. It needs someone who can keep the offense functional, protect the football and avoid turning…

title: 2 49ers, CeeDee Lamb fined in Niners vs. Cowboys
summary: The San Francisco 49ers saw two players issued fines in the aftermath of the Dallas Cowboys game last weekend as defensive backs Siran Neal and Marques Sigle were both flagged for infractions. Neal was fined $8,639 for an unnecessary roughness penalty, stemming from a punt return in the fourth quarter, where he was flagged for […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 4: Marques Sigle #36 of the San Francisco 49ers gets set during the fourth quarter of an NFL football game against the Denver Broncos at Levi's Stadium on October 4, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers saw two players issued fines in the aftermath of the Dallas Cowboys game last weekend as defensive backs Siran Neal and Marques Sigle were both flagged for infractions. Neal was fined $8,639 for an unnecessary roughness penalty, stemming from a punt return in the fourth quarter, where he was flagged for a facemask. The punt had initially pinned Dallas inside the 20, but Neal’s penalty on the tackle gave the Cowboys field position at their 34-yard line. Dallas would end up going 10 plays for 66 yards and a touchdown, cutting the lead to 38-32. Sigle was fined $6,142 for unnecessary roughness for a hit on a defenseless player. He was not flagged on the play, which came on a third-down incompletion early in the second quarter. Dallas would punt on the next play. Those weren’t the only two fines from the game. CeeDee Lamb was fined $23,882 for an illegal use of the helmet while delivering a block on Deommodore Lenoir on George Pickens’s 39-yard touchdown in the second quarter that put the Cowboys up 16-10. There was initially a flag thrown on the play, but it was picked up. #Cowboys WR CeeDee Lamb was fined $23,882 for illegal use of the helmet on this play. There was a flag thrown that was picked up. Looks like a shoulder hit to me 🤷🏻‍♂️ pic.twitter.com/JekeV9B018 — Mike Garafolo (@MikeGarafolo) November 21, 2026 On replay, it looked like Lamb delivered a hit with his shoulder to Lenoir’s shoulder on the block. He expressed frustration earlier in the week with the penalty when revealing he got fined. “I guess as a receiver, we can get hit, but can’t deliver the punishment,” Lamb said, via the Dallas News’s Joseph Hoyt. The 49ers ended up winning 46-40, and are now moving on to face the Minnesota Vikings this weekend, with kickoff set for 5:20 p.m. on Sunday night in Mexico City. Meanwhile, the Cowboys will face the Tennessee Titans at home, looking to bounce back from the loss.

title: 49ers waive Brandin Cooks, activate C.J. West
summary: The San Francisco 49ers made a pair of roster moves for their upcoming game against the Minnesota Vikings. They announced that they have activated defensive lineman C.J. West. To make room, they have waived wide receiver Brandin Cooks. Additionally, Cornerback Nate Hobbs has been downgraded to “out.” The Cooks waiver makes sense given that Mike […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - NOVEMBER 8: Brandin Cooks #84 of the San Francisco 49ers walks on the field during the first quarter of an NFL football game against the Las Vegas Raiders at Levi's Stadium on November 8, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers made a pair of roster moves for their upcoming game against the Minnesota Vikings. They announced that they have activated defensive lineman C.J. West. To make room, they have waived wide receiver Brandin Cooks. Additionally, Cornerback Nate Hobbs has been downgraded to “out.” The Cooks waiver makes sense given that Mike Evans is expected to play and De’Zhaun Stribling could return next month. I know some may want the 49ers to put Jacob Cowing on the chopping block, but it looks like Cooks is the odd man out. The 49ers probably didn’t want to make the decision after the Vikings game, as time was running out for West’s IR designation. West’s return will also help the defensive line, which had sack issues last week against the Dallas Cowboys. Whether you think that was blown out of proportion is up to you. West started in two games before his knee injury and was largely quiet. Now that his knee is healed, hopefully he can help the 49ers generate some significant pressure. With Hobbs being out, the 49ers have until Wednesday to make a decision . If they don’t activate Hobbs by then, his season is over. As for Cooks, he will need to clear waivers and then become a free agent. The 49ers could have a handshake agreement that, once he clears waivers, they’ll pick him back up for the practice squad, where he started his brief time with the team. Given all the time spent to get him up to speed on the offense, holding onto him in some way may be a smart move.

title: Mike Evans expected to play vs. Vikings after being listed questionable
summary: The San Francisco 49ers should have star wide receiver Mike Evans back for Sunday night against the Minnesota Vikings in Week 11, getting their top pass-catcher back after missing the last three games with an Achilles injury. NFL Network’s Mike Garafolo revealed that Evans is set to play, while sharing a link to a video […]
full_text: The San Francisco 49ers should have star wide receiver Mike Evans back for Sunday night against the Minnesota Vikings in Week 11, getting their top pass-catcher back after missing the last three games with an Achilles injury. NFL Network’s Mike Garafolo revealed that Evans is set to play, while sharing a link to a video from Evans’s agent, implying his return for Sunday night. Video from Mike Evans’ agent on Instagram. The #49ers WR is set for his return against the #Vikings tomorrow. https://t.co/IWErK9UYaQ — Mike Garafolo (@MikeGarafolo) November 21, 2026 Evans had been dealing with Achilles soreness for the past few weeks and finally returned to practice this week on Thursday. He practiced in limited fashion on Thursday and Friday before being ruled questionable by Kyle Shanahan going into the weekend. However, it looks like Evans will give it a go, providing the 49ers with some much-needed receiver help against their toughest test to date. His return means it’ll be the first game we see San Francisco’s new trio of wide receivers (Evans, Deebo Samuel, and Keenan Allen) work together. Samuel and Allen both shone last weekend against the Dallas Cowboys, with the former going for 109 all-purpose yards and two touchdowns, while the latter caught five passes for 61 yards on short notice. Thus far this season, in six games, Evans has 27 catches for 420 yards and three touchdowns. He did have his best two games of the season right before the injury, catching seven passes for 113 yards and a touchdown against the Seahawks, while grabbing three catches for 94 yards in just one half against Washington. Now, he’ll face an elite Vikings defense that has done a great job limiting top offenses this season.

title: The Death Zone: Where the 49ers-Vikings game gets decided
summary: In Mexico City, the San Francisco 49ers play football at 7,200 feet. The thinnest air on the field, though, will be in the last 20 yards. Climbers on Everest have a name for everything above 8,000 meters: the death zone. The body can’t adjust up there. It just runs out of time and air. And […]
full_text: (Photo by Adam Bettcher/Getty Images) In Mexico City, the San Francisco 49ers play football at 7,200 feet. The thinnest air on the field, though, will be in the last 20 yards. Climbers on Everest have a name for everything above 8,000 meters: the death zone. The body can’t adjust up there. It just runs out of time and air. And when researchers went back through decades of Everest deaths, the climbers who never made it home had the same things in common. They were exhausted. They fell behind. And they reached the top too late in the day. The red zone is football’s death zone. On Sunday, it could decide the game. The 49ers have scored touchdowns on 82.8% of their red zone trips this season, 24 of 29. According to The Associated Press, that’s the best rate of any offense since 2000. Brock Purdy has thrown 13 touchdowns inside the 20 and hasn’t been picked off once. The Minnesota Vikings allow touchdowns on 25% of red zone trips, the lowest rate of any defense over that same stretch. Two records. One summit. Don’t expect a shootout. Minnesota gives up 14 points a game, and the under has hit in eight of its nine games. Nights like this, you might only get three or four real shots at the top. Every drive is an expedition. The first downs are the base camps on the way up. The offensive line are the Sherpas, carrying the load so somebody else can stand on the summit. Nobody sprints up Everest. You climb it one camp at a time, and you don’t waste a step. Climbers start their summit push in the middle of the night, before the weather turns. Kyle Shanahan does the same thing with his opening script. The 49ers have scored on their first drive in seven of nine games this season: six touchdowns and a field goal. That’s the window before Flores has seen what’s coming. Brian Flores makes those last 20 yards feel like 8,000 meters. His defense blitzes more in the red zone than anyone, 70% of the time, per Next Gen Stats, and still plays more zone down there than anyone. He sends pressure and keeps bodies behind it. When the field shrinks, there’s nowhere left for the ball to go. By my count, when Minnesota has sent five or fewer rushers to rush inside its own 20 this season, quarterbacks have gone 6-for-20 for 30 yards. No touchdowns. Four sacks. An interception. But every mountain has a route. Both red zone passing touchdowns Minnesota has allowed in my count came when Flores sent six. When everybody comes, nobody’s left in the middle. Jared Goff found Jameson Williams. Jordan Love found Christian Watson. Quick, clean, gone. For the 49ers, the middle has a name. Against that six-man pressure this season, tight ends have caught four of the eight completions that went for 15 yards or more. Climbers carry oxygen for the final push. The 49ers carry George Kittle. Every Everest team sets a turnaround time. If you’re not on the summit by then, you turn back, no matter how close you are. On the mountain, turning around is how you live. Sunday night, it’s how you lose. Three points at the end of a 12-play climb is a turnaround, and the 49ers can’t afford many. They can’t afford any misses from Eddy Piñeiro, either, and he’ll have a little more range in the thin air. So avoid what kills climbers. Don’t wear down. Don’t fall behind, because third-and-long is where Flores’ six-man pressure is at its nastiest. And don’t get there late. It’s the matchup I’ve been circling all week on the show, and it’s the one that decides the game. Everest doesn’t care how good the climb was. It only cares who reaches the top. All season, nobody has done it better than the 49ers. On Sunday, nobody makes it harder than Minnesota.

Quick dump-offs to tight ends for eight-yard gains are big wins against this defense. To me, if you’re an EPA (big play) team, like the Packers, the Vikings are the worst possible matchup. Whereas a success-rate-driven offense, like the 49ers, can thrive against Minnesota. Love has been conditioned, by way of his offense, to hunt the big play. Brock Purdy is undoubtedly as aggressive, but there are far more built-in outs at every level in a Kyle Shanahan offense than there are in a Matt LaFleur offense. Green Bay had several plays where Dallas Turner or Andrew Van Ginkel were in a bind in coverage, but they couldn’t take advantage. Instead, Love was sacked because his eyes were downfield. Those will show up this week with Christian McCaffrey 1-on-1 in the open field, or Keenan Allen settling into the vacated area of a blitzer, or George Kittle and Deebo Samuel keeping the offense ahead of the chains on a screen pass.” Kyle Shanahan shares final updates ahead of 49ers-Vikings “I think it’s pretty easy just because of, it’s definitely easy for the coaches just because of what our schedule’s like. We’re leaving tomorrow morning, so I bet it hits them today, bet they’ll be ready to get out of here, but it’s been a great week. We haven’t felt any annoyance. Unless the 49ers start turning it over, he can get them to 20 or more points almost by himself against almost anybody. If the 49ers’ defense can hold Minnesota under that, they’ll get to 9-1 and on to a big home game against Seattle next weekend.” Five vital 49ers to watch vs. Vikings in Mexico City as NFC powerhouses collide “Minnesota blitzes on 78.6 percent of pass plays. That is nearly 30 percent higher than the next closest team in the NFL. But the Vikings don’t save their blitzes for just passing situations. They will test the 49ers on all downs, and San Francisco cannot afford any plays in which their offensive line is confused on their individual assignments.” The Cowboys might be ‘America’s Team.’ The 49ers aim to become the world’s team (paywall) “Offensive lineman Isaac Alarcon is from Monterrey, Mexico, while defensive tackle Sebastian Valdez’s parents were born in Mexico. He said an aunt, uncle and cousins will be at the stadium to cheer for him Sunday. “I grew up in San Diego, but I went to TJ (Tijuana) all the time,” he said. “And it just means a lot to my family and me to be able to represent my ethnicity, my culture and just show people it’s possible.” ….Their experience Down Under was so impressive that the 49ers are considering applying for marketing rights in Australia through the league’s Global Markets Program. They are also interested in expanding their footprint in Asian markets. The NFL has had to scuttle previous attempts to play games in China, but it remains on its radar, York said. He also noted the 49ers have played preseason games in Japan three times (1989, 1995 and 2002) and said, “I know Japan would like to have us back again.” “There’s some real interest in the NFL in the Philippines,” he added. “I don’t know if I can tell you that that’s the hottest next market, but we’re looking to do something in Asia.” 49ers’ Mike Evans on track to play vs. Vikings after missing past month with Achilles injury (paywall) “The 49ers will have a walk-through practice at the Air Force Academy on Saturday morning before departing for Mexico.” ‘It felt like a calling’: How 49ers’ Christian McCaffrey is fighting for veterans (paywall) “His foundation’s flagship initiative provides medical and mental-health care for Special Operations forces veterans suffering from post-traumatic stress. The program is run in conjunction with Resilience Code, whose founder, Dr. Chad Prusmack, has worked with McCaffrey for more than a decade on his athletic performance and cognitive function. McCaffrey approached Prusmack about creating comprehensive health evaluations for veterans, providing a year of no-cost personalized care. “Here I am getting the top care on planet Earth when it comes to my brain, my body, all these different images, blood work and access to treatment,” McCaffrey said. “The thought was: Why don’t we try to do as best we can to individualize plans for these men and women who have gone through so much?”

title: Where the 49ers need to improve defensively vs. Vikings
summary: Last weekend was not a good day for the San Francisco 49ers defense, as they gave up 40 points on the Dallas Cowboys, yet still managed to come away with the 46-40 victory. San Francisco’s defense struggled on all fronts. The secondary especially had its issues, as Dallas’s top three receivers all had quality games. […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TEXAS - NOVEMBER 15: Nick Bosa #97 of the San Francisco 49ers rushes the passer during a game against the Dallas Cowboys at AT&T Stadium on November 15, 2026 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images) | Getty Images Last weekend was not a good day for the San Francisco 49ers defense, as they gave up 40 points on the Dallas Cowboys, yet still managed to come away with the 46-40 victory. San Francisco’s defense struggled on all fronts. The secondary especially had its issues, as Dallas’s top three receivers all had quality games. George Pickens had 11 catches for 145 yards and three touchdowns, and that was with him dropping three passes. CeeDee Lamb had seven catches for 72 yards and a touchdown, while Ryan Flournoy had six catches for 71 yards and a touchdown. Cornerbacks Deommodore Lenoir, Renardo Green, and Upton Stout entered the game banged up, and it showed, as both had their fair share of struggles against Dallas’s elite offense. Of course, the matchup wasn’t easy facing a high-caliber quarterback with two Pro Bowl receivers, but it was a rough day for a defense that had been quite good over the first half of the season. That wasn’t the only issue. The 49ers pass rush was also ineffective, failing to sack Dak Prescott, and Nick Bosa came out this week and took accountability for his play this season. Bosa has yet to record a sack, although his other numbers still indicate a productive season, especially with the double teams and chips he’s facing. Now, this week, the health is looking better. Stout remained limited in practice with his ongoing shoulder injury and is questionable, but Lenoir wasn’t on the injury report and Renardo Green practiced in full on Thursday and is off the injury report for Sunday’s game. But the 49ers still have a tough challenge against the Minnesota Vikings, who put up 30 points on the Green Bay Packers in Kirk Cousins’s return. Minnesota’s offense suddenly looks formidable, and this battle should be a tough one on both sides. After their struggles against Dallas, where do the 49ers need to improve defensively against Minnesota? Ahead of Sunday night, defensive coordinator Raheem Morris broke down the main issues he saw from the Cowboys game and what to take from it. “Extending drives early with some of the penalties to get those guys to go down there, particularly on the first drive [was a problem]. We gave up three, I believe, on that first one,” Morris said. “We got the big penalty to get those guys down there. They got a big-time field goal kicker. A couple of big plays in the first half. The two big plays were the ones that killed us there early. Got a pretty good grip on it after that and kind of held it down. It was at some point it was like 38-19. Then that finishing moments, we didn’t do a very good job of getting the finishes off. Usually, the finishes happen when you’re able to generate pressure with sacks or you’re able to get interceptions. “The Cowboys did a nice job, to give them credit, of getting the ball out of their hand. Did a nice job of getting the ball into their good players’ hand, keeping drives going, extending drives. They had about three or four drives there where it was almost like overtime-like play for them, where it was going to be fourth down territory regardless and they were able to capitalize and go down and score on us. You would like to be able to stop some of those plays and be able to get those guys going and get off the grass at those moments and then that score wouldn’t have got to where it was, but those things didn’t happen. “We didn’t execute that way. And it’s a collective group. I know [Nick] Bosa stood up in front of you guys and took all the credit and took all the accountability, but I really think it’s just all of us. Some of it could be better play calls for them. Some of it could be better for us, what we can do for those guys. Some of it can be better plays made by us. Some of it, we just ran out a little bit of gas, got a little bit tired. Let’s not kid ourselves. Human nature as well. So, fortunate to get out of there with a win. Definitely want to learn those lessons when you get a chance to do those things in those moments, when you get wins. Something that we can learn from and grow from and something that we definitely will.” One thing Morris did see from his team was accountability after the game, with the leaders on the team stepping up. “They’re such an accountable group,” Morris added. “Most guys, you come in and you’re just upset after a game. These guys, they hold themselves to such a high standard. They come in, they’re able to speak very clearly right off the bat. So it’s not going to be more vocal the next week because they were vocal the first week. Not necessarily Bosa. Bosa’s kind of a to-himself guy, but for a guy like Fred [Warner], he’s always going to speak up and do the things that happened. It wasn’t like there was mistakes. They did some better job executing. There was a few mistakes. There’s always going to be mistakes and there’s always correcting mistakes. I’m not saying there’s not mistakes, but there’s always going to be correcting mistakes, but you correct those mistakes, you move on. “There’s some other things that, just you talking to as an individual player. The best thing about our guys, they always point at themselves first. Whether it’s Fred, whether it’s Bosa, whether it’s DMo (Deommodore Lenoir), Renardo [Green], anybody on our football team. That’s the cool part about being here with these guys is they point at themselves first. Then a lot of the times I’m able to say, ‘Hey, I can help you here’ or ‘we can do these things better. We can make these calls. We can help you out, do a little bit better in these situations.’ They are all so upfront and forthgoing with those things. That makes it really cool to talk to those guys that way.” Health seemed to be a factor last weekend, but the 49ers do need to be more disciplined and avoid the killer penalties (although some looked to be questionable calls). But there is a lot at stake this weekend for the 49ers, as their No. 1 seed odds shift dramatically with a win or a loss. San Francisco’s offense has always been up to the task, but they’ll get their toughest matchup of the year with Brian Flores’s defense. So, the 49ers defense will need to show up as well against this new-look Vikings offense with Kirk Cousins and execute on all three levels.

title: Commanders vs. Bengals injury report: Four key players questionable
summary: The Commanders listed four starters as questionable to play the Cincinnati Bengals on Monday night. The team formally made that announcement Saturday afternoon on their official injury report. Center Lucas Patrick (concussion), cornerback Amik Robertson (ankle) and running backs Rachaad White (heel) and Bill Croskey-Merritt (groin) received them, though not all questionable designations are equal […]
full_text: The Commanders listed four starters as questionable to play the Cincinnati Bengals on Monday night. The team formally made that announcement Saturday afternoon on their official injury report. Center Lucas Patrick (concussion), cornerback Amik Robertson (ankle) and running backs Rachaad White (heel) and Bill Croskey-Merritt (groin) received them, though not all questionable designations are equal in this instance. Head coach Dan Quinn essentially said that Patrick would start at center despite Nick Allegretti playing well in his absence. He was also optimistic about White, stating he skipped Saturday’s work to quiet some soreness in his heel. While Quinn wasn’t completely direct regarding White, it sure seems like he’s going to play. Robertson, however, is truly up in the air. He suffered an ankle injury on the last play of Friday’s practice and didn’t participate on Saturday. The Commanders will see how the ailment responds over the next few days before making a call on Robertson. If he can’t go, Rasul Douglas would play a lot more, with Mike Sainristil helping some in the slot. Croskey-Merritt was also listed as questionable to play the Bengals, though that designation is standard among players on injured reserve in their practice windows . The verdict on Croskey-Merritt’s status will come on Monday, when he’s activated (or not). After a week of full participation, it’s fair to expect Croskey-Merritt to be available. While receiver Treylon Burks was a DNP on Friday, it was an injury management play as he works to get his foot issue right. He didn’t receive a designation and will be available to play. Despite being limited during the practice week, safety Quan Martin (shoulder) will be available to play the Bengals. full_text: Dan Quinn spoke to reporters after the Washington Commanders finished their last full practice of the week. The team hosts the Cincinnati Bengals on Monday Night Football this week, and they’re coming off a mini-bye following last week’s Thursday Night Football win over the Giants. That break was good for the team’s injury report, as some players got a little healthier. The Commanders are still dealing with several injuries, including one that happened yesterday. CB Amik Robertson was seen limping after yesterday’s practice, and Quinn said he suffered a lower leg injury on the last play of the session. They’ll work with him over the next 48 hours to determine his game status for Monday night. Quinn said it would be a combination of Trey Amos and Rasul Douglas with Mike Sainristil and Fabian Moreau also getting reps on the inside if Robertson would miss time. Bill Croskey-Merritt is set to return from injured reserve after missing the last four games with a groin injury. Quinn wasn’t ready to committ to Bill playing Monday night, but he’s trending in the right direction and itching to get back on the field. Rachaad White didn’t practice today due to heel soreness, while WR Treylon Burks was back at practice and should be good to go with his lingering foot injury. Lucas Patrick suffered a concussion two weeks ago and was replaced by Nick Allegretti vs the Giants. That was the best the line and protections have looked in a while, but Quinn said the team is going back to Lucas now that he has cleared concussion protocol. Allegretti returns to a reserve role, able to back up the three interior OL positions. The game-winning touchdown drive in the final minutes was vintage Daniels — poised under pressure, decisive, and clutch when Washington needed him most. His PFF overall grade sits ninth among all 33 qualified quarterbacks in the league, and per PFF, the Daniels-to-Antonio Williams connection carries the second-highest passer rating pairing in the NFL. That’s not a coincidence; it’s a reflection of the route-running and timing chemistry those two have built week over week. The case to force him more targets Monday night is real. Against a Bengals defense that is at its best when it can tee off on a one-dimensional offense, David Blough needs to open the full playbook. That means rolling Daniels out, letting him threaten the edge, exploiting his clean-pocket advantage — PFF ranks him second among all quarterbacks when given a clean pocket — and creating the kind of open-space plays that make the Bengals’ pass rush irrelevant. Monday Night Football on a national stage with playoff hopes on the line. This is the kind of game Jayden Daniels has been building toward all season. Blough needs to trust him, give him room to operate, and let 5 be 5. The talent is there. The moment is here. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Hogs Haven The surprising key to victory over the Bengals Where does WAS have a competitive advantage? Believe it or not, the rushing attack. The Bengals are a poor rushing team, averaging 85 yards per game (30th), while Washington averages 117 (13th). And, for all the gnashing of teeth about the state of the offensive line and the running back stable, Washington is in the top 3rd of the league in rushing yards per attempt (4.3, tied for 11th with the Colts and Jonathan Taylor), while the Bengals are 23rd with 3.9 yards/attempt. Moreover, as I showed in the previous post, rushing defense is the key weakness of the Bengals: they currently rank 20th in rush yards against but 11th on passing yards against. Why play into their hands by getting into a passing showdown when the rushing attack is there for the taking? Remember that Washington abandoned its zone-heavy rushing attack last week in favor of duo (double team blocking on the IOL) and gap, the approaches used in the prior two years. That kind of attack recognizes the limitation of Paul at LG and their Centers as zone players and takes advantage of what they do best. (The other three linemen are zone versatile.) Well, guess what? Rachaad White is a star in duo and gap. In zone, which Washington has emphasized most of the year, White’s average yards per attempt is 3.93 and his success rate is 35% – far below average numbers in the NFL. But when he plays duo, he averages an elite 5.27 YPA and has a success rate of 55%. And when he plays gap, his YPA is an excellent 4.77 and his success rate is 54%. (Data in this paragraph are from Sumer Sports.). It looks like deemphasizing zone and focusing on duo and gap blocking not only fits the OL better, those schemes far better fit their leading rusher. If I’m the OC, I plan on running White at least 18-20 times, almost all in gap and duo. That could give him alone over 100 yards rushing. Doing so will make the play action game work far more effectively, will protect Daniels, will keep the game close, and will set up the kind of passes that can win a close game. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders WR Stefon Diggs on being confident the offense can keep up with the Bengals' offense pic.twitter.com/TfIcPmn8A7 — Martenzie Johnson (@10zJohnson) November 20, 2026 Washington Post (paywall) Cincinnati is contending again after recent struggles; can Jayden Daniels & Washington do the same? The Cincinnati Bengals nearly pulled it off. After the 2021 season, they made an improbable run to the Super Bowl before ultimately falling four points shy of upsetting the Los Angeles Rams. It was only quarterback Joe Burrow’s sophomore NFL season, which fed plenty of optimism about what they could accomplish before his big second contract hit the books. That hope wasn’t shaken when they fell to the eventual Super Bowl champion Kansas City Chiefs in the playoffs a year later. Cincinnati was viewed as a perennial contender that had plenty of financial flexibility to maximize its window. The Bengals haven’t made the postseason since. It wasn’t until this year that Cincinnati (7-2) would be regarded as a serious challenger again. The Washington Commanders (3-5-1) want to keep turning their season around when the teams meet Monday night at Northwest Stadium. The Commanders are rightfully focused on the present, not the big picture. That said, their opponent could provide some valuable long-term lessons. When assessing the Burrow-era Bengals’ winding path back to prominence, a road map emerges for the Jayden Daniels-era Commanders to do the same. title: Commanders favored to win NFC East in latest fan poll – survey results
summary: So, you’re telling me there’s a chance… Here’s what Ben Standig had to say earlier this week: The 2026 NFL regular season is past the halfway point, but the finish line remains too far away to make sweeping declarations about how the NFC East race will unfold. Suggesting that the eventual division winner will have […]
full_text: So, you’re telling me there’s a chance… Here’s what Ben Standig had to say earlier this week: The 2026 NFL regular season is past the halfway point, but the finish line remains too far away to make sweeping declarations about how the NFC East race will unfold. Suggesting that the eventual division winner will have at least eight victories doesn’t seem like a stretch, in theory. There’s a solid argument that the Washington Commanders are the best all-around team among the remaining contenders. (Step aside, Eagles.) Signs of life in a wide-open race When Washington sat at 1-3 following a dismal overseas loss to Indianapolis in Week 4, talk of an NFC East title felt like pure fantasy. Yet six games later, the burgundy & gold have quietly stitched together a 3-2-1 stretch highlighted by Thursday night’s 24-21 win over the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium that has breathed a sense of renewed optimism into at least part of the fan base. Now at 3-5-1, Washington still occupies third place in the division, trailing New York by 2 games. Even so, the underlying progress is real. Quarterback Jayden Daniels engineered a clutch late drive last Thursday night — connecting with Stefon Diggs on a 32-yard touchdown with 1:05 remaining — while Washington converted 7 of 14 third downs and held New York to 4-of-12 on third down. Moreover, over the past 6 games, the Commanders have largely protected the football — carrying a +7 turnover differential on the season while leaning on young contributors like tight end Ben Sinnott, wideout Antonio Williams, and cornerbacks Trey Amos and (the not-so-young) Amik Robertson. This week’s Reacts survey In this week’s Hogs Haven Reacts survey , we asked readers two questions to gauge the community’s temperature entering Week 11. The first was our weekly benchmark: Are you confident in the overall direction of the team? This week, 46% of respondents answered “Yes,” while 54% voted “No”. That 32-point surge from last week’s 14% approval mark mirrors the 21-point jump we saw in Week 9 after Washington beat the Eagles. Nothing cures midweek angst quite like beating a division rival in prime time! Still, the fact that 54% of voters remain in the “No” camp shows that skepticism runs deep. As several commenters and fans have mentioned, Washington has yet to beat a clear playoff contender outside of Seattle in Week 3, and they let winnable games against the Colts and Giants slip away earlier in the fall. Until the Commanders can achieve sustained winning, a majority of the fan base is keeping its guard up, and the heat will stay turned up on head coach Dan Quinn and GM Adam Peters. A massive swing in the NFC East outlook Our second question asked which team respondents believe will win the NFC East division title in 2026. Despite Washington sitting behind both New York and Dallas in the standings, the results were fairly decisive: Visit our partners at FanDuel That 54% vote represents a dramatic reversal from earlier in the season, but it stems less from sudden perfection in Ashburn than from the vulnerabilities of Washington’s rivals. The Giants First, Washington owns the head-to-head tiebreaker over the Giants (5-3-1) after Thursday’s win. Second, the schedule-makers did New York no favors. Over the final 8 weeks, the Giants must run a gauntlet that includes Jacksonville, San Francisco, Seattle, and Detroit, whereas Washington gets much softer matchups against Arizona, Tennessee, and Atlanta. The Cowboys Meanwhile, Dallas (4-6) has been unable to win back-to-back games since November 28, 2025, and its defensive struggles reached a boiling point this week when head coach Brian Schottenheimer stripped first-year coordinator Christian Parker of play-calling duties in favor of senior defensive assistant Mike Pettine. To beat out Washington for the division title, the Cowboys will have to win as many times in their remaining 7 games as the Commanders win in their final 8. Don’t forget that the Commanders still have a chance to inflict a loss on the Cowboys when they meet in Landover for the final game of the regular season in Week 18. How can Washington win the division? The math is straightforward: if Washington can match the win totals of both the Giants and Cowboys, the Commanders will be the division winner! Washington holds the tiebreaker over the Giants, and, because of the Week 5 tie, matching Dallas in the win column would put Washington a half-game ahead of the silver & blue. If, for example, the Commanders can win 5 of their final 8 games to finish 8-8-1, they would be division champs if the Giants go 3-5 and the Cowboys, who have only 7 games remaining, finish out the season 4-3. Of course, with 8 weeks to go, there are sure to be a lot of twists & turns before things are decided, but the Cowboys’ games in Week 17 vs the Giants and Week 18 on the road against the Commanders could prove to be decisive in determining the ultimate division champ. Two camps in the comments Readers in the survey article comment thread broke cleanly along familiar lines. The optimistic Pollyanna camp — voiced by Savo_UK , Redskins21Life , and BillWard among others– pointed directly to the schedule imbalance. Their consensus is that if Washington takes care of business against Arizona, Tennessee, Atlanta, and Dallas (in Week 18), stealing just 1 upset against Cincinnati, Houston, Minnesota, or Jacksonville would be enough to reach 8 wins, which could be enough to claim the division in this 2026 season. The skeptical Cassandra camp — led by theFan4Life , WillThomas , and Greengmork among others — warned against mistaking a single prime-time escape against the Giants for a turnaround. They argue that Washington’s defense still struggles to generate consistent pressure, that the roster lacks the talent to beat playoff-caliber offenses, and that finishing around .500 risks trapping the franchise in draft-position purgatory without building a true contender. My take from the cheap seats As usual, I see the glass half-full. Defensively I think the Commanders defense has looked completely different since the return of Nick Cross and Trey Amos to the lineup. In the first 5 games of 2026, the Commanders surrendered an average of 29.8 points per game. Since Week 6 in San Francisco, when Amos and Cross took the field together for the first time, Washington has given up 18.5 points per game. While that stretch did include games against the struggling Eagles and last week’s road trip to New York, it also included games against the Niners and Rams. While passing yards surrendered since Week 6 are not dramatically improved (255 per game in Wks 1-5; 232 per game in Wks 6-10), the number of passing TOUCHDOWNS surrendered has changed dramatically, from 2.8 per game (14 total) in the first 5 weeks to 0.75 per game (3 total) in the four most recent games; the secondary has not allowed more than one passing touchdown in any of those contests. Game-by-Game Breakdown Weeks 1–5 Week 1 at Eagles (L 24–22): 182 net yds (203 gross), 3 TDs Week 2 at Cowboys (L 37–20): 266 net yds (279 gross), 4 TDs Week 3 vs. Seahawks (W 33–31): 393 net yds (393 gross), 4 TDs Week 4 vs. Colts (L 30–13): 129 net yds (143 gross), 0 TDs Week 5 vs. Giants (T 27–27): 305 net yds (326 gross), 3 TDs Weeks 6–10 (Bye in Week 7) Week 6 at 49ers (L 23–17): 249 net yds (264 gross), 1 TD Week 8 vs. Eagles (W 27–10): 177 net yds (212 gross), 0 TDs Week 9 vs. Rams (L 20–13): 219 net yds (228 gross), 1 TD Week 10 at Giants (W 24–21): 283 net yds (293 gross), 1 TD Anyone looking at the full-season stats for Washington’s pass defense would question the Commanders’ ability to limit the Bengals’ high-powered attack this week. But a look at the most recent 4 games — which include playing against Matt Stafford & Puka Nacua as well as Brock Purdy and the Kyle Shanahan offense — might well bolster the confidence of Commanders fans with respect to improvements in Washington’s pass defense since Cross and Amos took the…

title: Why Daronte Jones has Washington Commanders defense trending up
summary: Commanders defensive coordinator Daronte Jones sent two extra pass rushers at Giants quarterback J.J. McCarthy on a key third down midway through the fourth quarter.   He got burned for it.   Blitzing linebacker Frankie Luvu got picked up in protection. Nick Cross did not, but the unblocked safety hesitated just enough to let the […]
full_text: Commanders defensive coordinator Daronte Jones sent two extra pass rushers at Giants quarterback J.J. McCarthy on a key third down midway through the fourth quarter. He got burned for it. Blitzing linebacker Frankie Luvu got picked up in protection. Nick Cross did not, but the unblocked safety hesitated just enough to let the ball get out. The result was disastrous, with Sonny Styles going for an interception instead of a sure tackle — he probably picks it a year from now — that allowed Isaiah Likely to make a catch and run for a 66-yard touchdown that gave New York the lead. JJ McCarthy to Isaiah Likely for a 66 yard TOUCHDOWN!!! GIANTS UP! pic.twitter.com/s9nKBAzkaF — Bobby Skinner (@BobbySkinner_) November 13, 2026 That could’ve represented a traumatic event that changed Jones’ play calling. It didn’t. He kept the pedal to the floor, sending one blitz after another. The waves of pressure forced two three-and-outs and a Rasul Douglas interception – Jones sent six on that play — that sealed a 24-21 victory that saved Washington’s season. RASUL DOUGLAS CALLS GAME. pic.twitter.com/5q7ahQYaoa — NFL (@NFL) November 13, 2026 It also signaled that the Commanders defense is trending in the right direction. There was, however, nowhere to go but up. Washington gave up 29.8 points per game in their first five games. They have given up 18.5 points per game in their last four. While there’s plenty to clean up, especially in terms of explosive pass plays allowed, the Commanders are taking the ball away and getting home more often. “You’re starting to see guys play with more confidence,” Jones told on-site reporters during his weekly press conference. “They’re starting to understand where their help is going to be and the importance of the details. … Like anything, when you have some type of success and you’re getting the ball off of guys, you start building more confidence. You can see the guys playing more comfortable with what we’re asking them to do. “Continuing to progress in that way is what we’re looking for. …Guys are starting to see what it should look like on tape.” Those are encouraging signs, especially after how the season started. A learning curve was always expected when dealing with Jones’ scheme, a blitz-heavy system that disguises pressure and requires tons of communication and pre-snap adjustments. It’s a high-risk, high-reward system that, when executed well, can be hard to handle. Just look at the Vikings’ system it’s based on and run by Jones’ mentor, Brian Flores. The Commanders don’t have Minnesota’s talent or similar experience running the scheme, so different results are expected. The Commanders rank third in blitz rate at 42.1% and are No. 19 in pressure rate at 35.1%, but blitzes are starting to work better. Jones also believes there are two parts to every pass play, with what happens before and after the ball is thrown. Washington must be good in both areas to be successful within the system. Improvement in those areas comes down to the details. “The more they’re focused on that, it trims down the errors,” Jones said. “The margin of error is so small, and our ability to be focused in that way is some of the things you’re seeing. Also, I think the guys are starting to feel confident in what we’re asking them to do. They’re feeling confident with what their assignment is and how we’re asking them to play. “They’re continuing to dial in on those techniques and fundamentals within the details of the scheme. You’re starting to see that come to life. There are naturally some growing plans, but the fact the guys are still progressing — that’s what we’re looking for as a coaching staff.” Jones has also adjusted to the talent around him, playing more to their strengths. Head coach Dan Quinn said Jones has “taken a layer or two out” to help ease the execution. Washington’s defense will be tested by the Cincinnati Bengals offense, which has scored 30-plus points in their last five games. Quarterback Joe Burrow might be this defense’s kryptonite, considering how well he and the Bengals coaching staff handles the blitz. Burrow has the third-highest success rate when facing five rushers or more and has the NFL’s highest completion rate at 73.4% against the blitz. Also, Jones said that Cincinnati prioritizes protection and does a good job disguising their work in pass pro. Does all that impact how Jones will call Monday night’s game? He isn’t volunteering that. He did provide the primary objective, to keep Burrow off balance. “We have to, in some way shape or form, provide mental stress,” Jones said. “He can’t be sitting back there knowing our coverage. We have to find a way to change the picture. It’s going to become a chess match.” How will the Commanders defense fare against Joe Burrow and the Bengals? Will Daronte Jones blitz him a ton? Let us know in the comments below:

title: Cardinals rule out rookie Carson Beck, turn to 40-year-old Josh Johnson vs. Chiefs
summary: Cardinals rookie quarterback Carson Beck has been downgraded to out, paving the way for 40-year-old Josh Johnson to start against the Chiefs.
full_text:
Cardinals rookie quarterback Carson Beck has been downgraded to out for Sunday's game against the Chiefs , paving the way for 40-year-old Josh Johnson to get his first start for Arizona.
Coach Mike LaFleur said Friday that Arizona was preparing Johnson to start after Beck experienced back spasms again this week. Beck didn't practice Thursday or Friday after being a limited participant Wednesday.
Sunday against the Chiefs at Arrowhead Stadium will be Johnson's first start since Week 18 of last season and just his 12th career start after being a fifth-round pick in 2008. He is 2-9 overall.
Although he doesn't have a lot of starting experience compared with his longevity in the league -- Arizona is his 15th NFL team -- the situation Johnson is in feels "familiar."
"It's kind of my testimony my whole life, just the unknown, what can happen," Johnson said. "And so just always just being in the moment, being prepared for myself. I've been in this situation, particularly in the NFL, a lot. So more excited than nerves, I would say."
Johnson said he is in a constant state of staying ready, which has been a factor in him playing into his 40s. At this point in his career, he's used to it.
Last season, Johnson replaced injured Washington Commanders quarterback Marcus Mariota in Week 16 and then started the final two games of the season after not starting since 2021.
"My job is to always be ready no matter what, no matter how the situation," Johnson said. "So I focus more on that than what's not ideal. And so this is just the next step of that process, and it keeps happening and so you just keep accepting it. You don't fight it, you embrace it, and you just go with it."
Johnson said his experience working with LaFleur in 2020 when LaFleur was the San Francisco 49ers ' receivers coach and in 2021 with the New York Jets when LaFleur was the offensive coordinator will help "tremendously" on Sunday.
"Just understanding how he calls the game first and foremost is very important because you don't have to get antsy, like, 'Oh, what is he going to do in these moments?'" Johnson said. "And Mike is pretty consistent. He's been consistent. I've always been a big fan of him as a playcaller, as a coach, just in general."
Johnson is also familiar with Chiefs defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo, having played against him and being on the Giants when Spagnuolo was New York's defensive coordinator in 2016.
Despite a familiarity and comfort with LaFleur, Johnson is also realistic about how Sunday can go after spending less than two weeks learning the offense.
"I also understand that everything ain't going to be perfect," Johnson said. "I'm not trying to go out there and be perfect. I'm trying to go out there and play winning football."

title: NFL Week 11 uniforms: Texans debut Rivalries look, Commanders rock 'Hail Raiser'

full_text:
A primetime game can be a perfect opportunity for a team to send a message with its play. It also helps when it is looking its finest on the gridiron. The Houston Texans and Washington Commanders enter Week 10 with one part of that down with the debut of their respective uniforms.

 

 It was the Texans' turn first, as they wore their Rivalries threads against the Indianapolis Colts on "Thursday Night Football." The look is primarily white, but includes H-Town blue and battle red with details that pay homage to Houston's streets. The city's signature blue street tiles appear on the uniform's helmet, name plate, sleeve, collar and pant stripes in a two-tone battle red and blue finish. Houston's "be someone" bridge is the inspiration for the blue jersey numbers.

 For the first time, the Texans wore a liberty white helmet, paying tribute to the white prototype founder Robert C. McNair revealed in 1999 before shifting to a deep steel blue lid. The white helmet's face mask includes a chrome H-town blue finish, a nod to Houston's car culture. 

 As part of the Commanders' redesign of their uniform closet last offseason , they unveiled the all-black "Hail Raiser" alternates, which debut against the Cincinnati Bengals on "Monday Night Football." It features a black helmet with a "Spear W" logo on both sides, as the spear and "W" are interwoven at their center. Burgundy and gold stripes appear on the sleeve and pants, while the lid includes a three-stripe look on top of similar colors. Solid burgundy block numbers are outlined by gold. 

 The Buffalo Bills are also rocking a Rivalries look against the Miami Dolphins . Buffalo debuted its all-white "Cold Front" combination last season, but it returns with icy details throughout. The shoulder sleeve features a chrome charging buffalo, the first time a Bills uniform incorporates this element. The white helmet similarly includes a frosty metallic-filled charging buffalo logo, while the shoulder and pant leg patters boast a cracked-ice texture with a pattern that resembles snowfall on a bison's fur.

Complete with a Honolulu blue matte helmet, the "Motor City Muscle" threads were first unveiled in 2024. The lid also includes a leaping lion logo in silver with a black stripe down the middle.
